speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. J. D. F. DRUMMOND, M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the third time, within less than a month, it is my painful duty to be called upon to refer at the opening of Monday's proceedings, to the removal by the hand of death, during the brief adjournment over the week-end, of an hon. member of this House.
Three weeks ago it was hon. members on this side of the House who were bereaved of one of their numbers; last week, it was hon. gentlemen immediately opposite; to-day it is the leader and members of the Progressive party. In each instance, death followed swiftly upon a brief illness.
John Douglas Fraser Drummond, who died in this city yesterday afternoon, was the member for West Middlesex, in this province. He was in his sixty-sixth year. Mr. Drummond was one of the best-known farmers of western Ontario. He started farming as a boy on his father's farm in Middlesex, and attained marked success in mixed farming and in the raising of grade Durham cattle. He became actively identified with the United Farmers' movement when it took its rise in the province a few years ago, and at the last general election was returned to this parliament, defeating nominees of both the Liberal and Conservative parties.
Mr. Drummond's life rvas continuously associated with the interests of agriculture and the county he represented, which was also the county of his birth. Before entering federal politics he had during a period of thirty years, been successively councillor, reeve and clerk of his native township, having held the latter office for sixteen years.
Greatly respected by all who knew him, and especially by hon. members of this House, the country loses in the death of the hon. member a well-informed and faithful representative of its agricultural interests in parliament, and the constituency of West Middlesex one of her best-known and most devoted sons.	'
The sympathy of hon. members of this House will go out in fullest measure to the widow and others of the family of our late fellow-member who have been so suddenly and so greatly bereaved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. J. D. F. DRUMMOND, M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be borne home upon all of us that the passing of eleven of our number in the short space of three years and four months emphasizes the uncertainty and the hazardous character of human life. I do not think that within any period of our history so many have been called in the duration of a single parliament. All of the hon. members who have gone were men of quiet, unpretentious demeanour and, with the exception of two, took no very ostentatious part in the affairs of this parliament. If they had infirmities they kept them to themselves. This was very em-
Customs Act

phatically the case as respects the hon. member for West Middlesex who, with tragic suddenness, was taken from us just yesterday morning.
As he came from that portion of the province in which I was born and brought up, I can well understand the type represented by Mr. Drummond. He was of that hard-headed, firm-principled group of men of Scotch descent who mainly settled western Ontario and to whom that favoured section of Canada owes to-day its greatness and its wealth. Mr. Drummond gained early in his career the confidence of his fellows, and carried that confidence into a wider sphere. I am sure we all concur in the graceful tribute of the Prime Minister, and to-day I can only add that among his associates in the House the same opinion was formed of his character and attainments as that gained by him in the section in which he was born. We on this side join hon. gentlemen opposite in sympathy with our friends to the left and extend to them, and still more to his family and to his neighbours, the expression of our deep regret for his loss and our sincere appreciation of his valuable labours in this House.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. J. D. F. DRUMMOND, M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) I desire to associate myself with the words spoken by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, and to join with them in their tribute to one of our number who has been called from our midst by death. The news of Mr. Drummond's death reached us with painful-shall	I say tragic?-suddenness.
Many of us were unaware until two days ago that he was ill; none of us realized that the illness was of a serious character, or one from which he might not speedily recover. The late member for West Middlesex was a quiet, sincere, unassuming man who undertook his work here seriously, and sought to accomplish it fearlessly and conscientiously. After years of service in the municipal sphere he entered this House at an age when a man less public spirited might think of retirement, ease and seclusion. He did so in an attempt to serve his fellow men. In that service he was stricken, and in the service of his country many miles from the home in which he lived, and many miles from his loved ones, he died. That the strain imposed upon him by his duties here in no small measure contributed to that physical collapse from which his strength did not enable him to recover no one will dispute. It is, with feelings of profound regret, mingled1 with that sense of 
sorrow and sadness inseparable from the severance of friendship's ties by death, that we, the members of the group to which he belonged, with those who have already spoken, ask you to convey to his sorrow-stricken widow, and to the members of the bereft family our most sincere and heartfelt sympathy.

It is absolutely necessary that they should register and be given a number so that if anything goes wrong in the case of butter on the export market we can trace it right back to the very factory from which it came, and the very vat in which it was made.

I think the hon. member for Comox-AIberni (Mr. Neill) is absolutely correct. All he wanted, and all that any of us wanted, at the time the discussion took place, was to make it clear that while this grading should apply to butter or other products which ought not to be exported, in a word, to bad produce, a certificate should not be refused on any other ground except that the produce was bad. We suggested at the time that the provision should read:
For refusing to grade dairy produce deemed unfit or unsuitable for export.
That was the only ground on which the minister himself thought the grading should be refused. This amendment is simply for the purpose of showing clearly that this grading shall only be refused in connection with butter which should not be exported.

Let me repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the reason I have given is only one illustration [why we should have the power to refuse to grade. In committee we went very fully into all the other reasons. For instance, suppose the producer refused to subscribe to the Requirement in regard to the character of the boxes or the hoops to be used, or any other provision of the law and so tend to prejudicially affect our dairy products in the Old Country market, how are we going to get at him? A mere nominal fine will not bring him to time. We must in some way protect the rest of the dairymen; those who observe the law should not suffer from the odium incurred by reason of the conduct of one or two offenders. This is a power which we are exercising now, and we exercise it quite frequently in the case of cheese sent to Montreal, or any other point where there is cold storage and where we have graders.	If the cheese is only three
or four days old we refuse absolutely to grade it until the product is sufficiently
Dairy Produce Act

ripened to be worthy of the name of cheese. We are exercising this power now, but we really have no legal authority for doinig so. If some person challenged our right to refuse to grade green cheese it would be found that we do not have that power under the law. However we are acting on the assumption that we have the power; and we reserve to ourselves the discretionary right not to grade green cheese until, at least, it is ten or twelve days old. Therefore we are only asking, in this section, the right to do what we are actually doing at the present time. As a matter of fact nobody has taken exception to our exercising that authority. However, supposing they did object and brought suit against us for not grading this green cheese when it was three or four days old, seeing that we are without any authority, we might lose the case before the courts. And yet it would be quite unfair to the legitimate makers of cheese that the grade should be issued when cheese was green. You cannot give a grade to cheese when it is green; at that time it is not cheese but simply pressed curd. It took about a year to get our creameries to register. The committee will remember that about two years ago a certain sample of butter was put on the market in Great Britain and was reported in the press as having made people sick. Doctors were called in and they discovered bacteria in it. Do hon. members mean to say that a creamery should be allowed to turn out a product that was going to prejudice the entire trade of Canada?
Certainly not.

No. We should
have the discretionary power. When the whole trade of the country is in danger we should have the power, not only to fine a man and correct the difficulty, but we should be able, if a man persisted, to stop him altogether. This provision only applies to export butter. Occasionally a man voluntarily comes to us and asks for a grade for butter for home consumption. We have very rarely given it; if we have time we give the grade, but if not we do not grade it.

The minister's explanations
are entirely apart from the line of argument I am trying to present. I am not objecting to his refusing export certificates for any product whatever. He does it every day in the week, and it is quite all right, so far as I am con-cemed'; but I object to the department taking arbitrary power to refuse to grade the dairy products of any man because they do not like the colour of his hair or the place he comes

from. If they do not like a man they can Say to him, "I will not grade your products." The minister reads into the act something that is not there. He says we are only going to apply this provision to a man who habitually breaks the law and going to say to him, "Now we are tired of you, and will not grade your butter." But the act will also apply to the man who never had any produce graded. They may give some extraordinary reason, or none at all, and say to the man, "I will not grade your butter." That is not compatible with our ideas of justice. The remedy is to refuse to give him an. export certificate. The minister says that is no punishment, because he will pay the fine; but if the man cannot export his product, he will very soon get tired of producing it, because if he cannot ship it he will have to take it home. There is nothing profitable to him in that. Paying the fine is not the principal thing, it is the loss of the shipment and being compelled to dispose of it in some other way; and if his product is continually rejected on account of being an inferior grade, he will stop trying to export it in a very short time.
Then another point: How is a man to know why his produce is rejected, if you refuse to grade it? They may say it is rejected because it is not a good product, but how do they know that? The product should be graded, and if it is inferior it should be rejected. That will penalize a man far more than a fine. But it is not fair to say "I will refuse to grade your product." Suppose a man, through the carelessness of his servants, has made one or two inferior shipments and they have been rejected. That is no reason why he should be put out of business. If a man reforms, intends to do better, and to exercise more care, he should be allowed an opportunity to go on. I observe a great deal of the legislation proposed by the Department of Agriculture is framed along the same lines and extremely arbitrary; they take upon themselves a power which no other department ever assumes. It may be that there js a lack of co-ordination between the Legal branch and the Department of Agriculture. Time and again we have had occasion to protest against the arbitrary powers assumed by some branch or other of the Department of Agriculture.

We are endeavouring to raise the quality of good exportable farm products, and in doing that we increase the temptation to people to try to export inferior goods, and that means that we must have more restriction. There is not one-half

Dairy Produce Act
the arbitrary provisions in this law that you will find in the Australian or New Zealand laws.
It is not a restriction; it is a prohibition.

We do not say that we do not propose to grade anything because it is bad. We will grade the butter, as long as it is what it pretends to be. But if a man sends over adulterated butter, we have to prosecute him, and if he persists-and only under those circumstances-we decline to grade.

That is not put in the act.
Mr, MOTHERWELL: That is the fact. Take the other illustration in regard to cheese. I submit that you cannot specify all the offences imaginable. If you try to do so, something else crops up and you cannot deal with it. I was illustrating that with regard to cheese that was found to have certain bacteria existing in it which allegedly endangered the life of certain parties who ate it. We have a bacteriologist who has been placed in charge to look after such things. If the man who sent the allegedly dangerous cheese had been allowed to continue his shipments he might have hurt our cheese trade, and if we are going to do justice to the cheese men of the country we must have this authority; there is no question about that.
Then with regard to registration: It was with the greatest difficulty that we prevailed upon the creamery and cheese faetor:es to register. No registration fee was charged an;! all they were asked to do was to send their address and location and we would allot them a number. Having the number, it is possible to trace any cheese or butter back to the factory. If the factory persists in not having itse'f numbered or identified, we say, " All right, you persist in the refusal to register, ' and we will have *to decline to grade your produce ", That is not unreasonable. If my hon. friend thinks it would be providing any safeguard to say that this does not apply to butter for home consumption, I have no objection, but there will be a danger in that.

I think we all agree with everything. the minister says, except the application he seeks to make of what he says to the subject before him. He does not want to do any injustice to anybody, and only desires to refuse grades for produce which is not a good quality, and to refuse certificates to those who habitually break the law. But why does he not say so? That wou'd be the easiest thing' in the world. We
have the two points before us, and I think the protest of my hon. friend (Mr. Neill) is absolutely right. I do not know why the minister objects to it because what he asks is simply to put in writing what the minister says in words.
We have it.

No, what we
have here is something which would enable the department to withhold a certificate without any conditions, for any possible earthly reason, or for absolutely no reason at all. Surely that is not good legislation.

Would my hon.
friend suggest that we enumerate the number of offences?

No. In the first place two things came up. The first was the article itself. As regards the refusal to grade dairy produce, the word "grade" there, I assume, is not the testing of the butter but is used in the technical sense that after testing the butter, you give it an appropriate grade?
Yes.

Of course, unless we use the word in that sense, the sentence would have no real meaning, because refusal to grade would mean refusal to consider, and I apprehend that is not what is meant. What is meant is that after the inspection is made and the test made, the appropriate grade is to be given. After the minister says that after that is done, they should have the right to say there shall be no grade at alii and refuse all grades. He says: they should have that right because, if not, unfit produce may be exported to the harm of our whole export business. He is absolutely right. The claim is made that .we should show what we are doing in using the word "grade" in the sense the minister uses it in his draft bill. He will get around that point entirely by inserting after the word "produce" simply the following amendment:
Deemed unfit or unsuitable for export.
Paragraph (g) will then read:
For refusing to grade dairy produce deemed unfit or unsuitable for export.
That is all he says he wants. I am taking him at his word. Then again he says: "But there is another case than the grading of the article itself. We want to be in a position to police people who will not properly carry on business. They may have a good article that ought to be graded, but they may do this, that or the other thing which renders it dangerous for us to give them a grade at all."
Dairy Produce Act

He says: That applies in the case of a man who habitually pays no attention to our regulations. Again that can be clearly shown. If clearly shown, the sentence would read thus:
And for withholding grade certificates to any person habitually guilty of disregarding the regulations under this aot.
That is what my hon. friend says he wants to do. He says he wants to be fair to the trade. Why not do that? It covers both of his points.

I think the situation can be met by a simpler amendment than that suggested by the hon. member. If we strike out the first seven words in paragraph (g), that will meet the whole situation. The minister will then be given power to withhold export certificates because the certificates are for export. A man cannot export butter unless he has an export certificate. If that is withheld the whole situation is met. The minister does not need power to refuse to grade. Such power might be used in a very arbitrary manner and there is no necessity for it. The explanation given on the right-hand page reads:
If such butter and cheese is not graded, and no certificate issued, it cannot be exported.
Let me read this again in a different way:
If such butter and cheese has no export certificate issued, it cannot be exported.
Refusal to grade is not needed at all So long as you keep it from going out of the country, that will settle the situation as regards export. It will punish the man and prevent him from committing the offence again.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the word "export" be inserted?

I would strike out the first seven words of paragraph (g) and make it read like this:
For withholding export certificates.

There is not very much difference. I have tried to assure my hon. friend1 that this is only for export but if he would feel better satisfied if the words "for export" were inserted, there will be no objection.

Insert the word "export"
instead of "grade."
Why not make it read:	"For refusing to grade dairy produce and for withholding grade certificates for export"?

My whole case is my
objection to giving power to refuse to grade butter for any man. That is an arbitrary fSir Henry Drayton.]
power. The minister says that he will not exercise it except under certain conditions, but those conditions are not stated in the legislation. He is taking full power to refuse to grade perhaps an honest man's honest butter because, he says-this power is sometimes required. That is not the way to handle the situation. The object is to prevent bad butter from being exported and this can be met by making paragraph (g) read:
For withholding export certificates.

Again I assure my hon. friend that the question is not whether the butter is bad or good. The British market will consume anything that is fit for human consumption. When a man finds it more profitable to continue to commit an offence and to pay the fine so long as he can export, we want to say that he cannot export. There may be a dozen offences of this nature. We are exercising this power now and1 unless we have this legislation, somebody is going to challenge our power and we shall find that the door will be open to all kinds of exportable stuff. No arbitrary power has. been or is being exercised in this matter, and the law is not one-half as strict as the laws of either New Zealand or Australia. Unless we tighten up our laws in many other respects, we are going to find our export in many other commodities will be gravely jeopardised by dishonest exporters.

What more power could
the minister need than when he has full arbitrary power to withhold a certificate for export? We have not the laws of New Zealand here for purposes of comparison. It is a standard argument. that something else is done somewhere else. So long as we give the minister or his agents precise power to forbid any export, surely he does not want any more than that. He has the power to refuse any export certificate. Is that not sufficient? No, he says, in addition to that I will say to Tom Jones:	"I will not grade your
butter." Is that fair?

We threshed this
matter out pretty fully in the Agriculture committee and there was not a single dissenting voice. If the matter were otherwise, I would be disposed to ask that the committee rise and we discuss this further with my hon. friend because I do not think he understands the question at issue. But in view of the unanimity in the Agriculture committee and the fact that we are exercising this power now, I think that we should proceed with the bill. It is simplicity itself-the right to withhold a certificate from offenders of the law, as for instance, men who deliber-

Meat and Canned Foods Act
ately refuse to register their factories. There are probably half a dozen other reasons. The thing is so elementary in its rightness. We should know now whether the department should have that power or not. If we cannot get that power and are assuming the right to exercise a power we do not possees, what will happen? We shall be unable to prevent goods being sent abroad that will do harm to our export business. I do not want to see that, and I do not think the committee wants it. No specific power is given now and we are merely exercising it without legislation. There is no complaint of abuse. Why should we abuse it? We are, if anything, erring on the side of leniency.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

The House resumed from May 11 consideration in committee of Bill No. 73, to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act-Hon. Mr. Motherwell-Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-"Canned foods".
Does this apply to canned salmon?
It was my under standing, and I think I am right in saying that it does not.

"Canned foods", according to this section, includes "foods that have been pre-heated, cooked, preserved, condensed", and so on. If that does not cover salmon I should like to know why, how or where it does not.
I understand that there is another act relating to salmon. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) asked me the same question on a previous occasion. I wonder whether he has looked the matter up.

Would it cover
canned sardines?
It does not apply to fish at all.

The minister will recall that on two previous occasions I drew his attention to this matter, not for the purpose of interfering with the passage of this legislation but because this is of some importance. We are passing a good deal of legislation of this character, some of which is regarded as harassing to business, although I am not saying that this is. We shall wake up to find, if this bill passes that under its powers the inspectors will be dealing with canned salmon as well as with canned foods generally. The section clearly refers to foods of all kinds.
I will let the section stand.
The pure food law is the one to which the minister refers.
Would the section apply to canned tomatoes?

I think we had better let it stand.
Section stands

Meat and Canned Foods Act
On section 2-Canned fruit or vegetables or foiod to be offered for sale in prescribed containers only.

Heretofore the containers have been specified by dimensions but the specific gravity of the contents varying, the weight would vary, so that although a tin by measurement might be supposed to contain four pounds, the contents would not be quite up to that weight. It was therefore necessary that the containers should bear a label indicating that the weight was so much, less so many ounces. Now, instead of having the containers conform to a certain size, we are providing that the contents must weigh so much net. In the case of grain, a bushel of wheat might weigh more or less than a bushel of some other product; just the same as a bushel measure of potatoes will hold a very different weight from a bushel measure of wheat. So a four-pound syrup container, while it will hold this weight when the syrup is thick, will not when the syrup is thin. Consequently, with the specific gravity of these commodities varying so much, we find we cannot protect the public by specifying a certain size of tin; the only way is by prescribing that the tin must contain so many pounds net.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, what the minister says about the meaning of the term "food or food products." If the question is open under the first section, it must also be open under the second1.

The principle
embodied in the second section is the size.

Yes, but it
applies to any food or food products just as much as the preceding section does.
Why should it not apply to all foods?

I am not
answering my hon. friend's question; I had not anything to do with the preparation of the bill, and that was not the subject of my inquiry. Recently an hon. gentleman interested in the fish business-probably my hon. friend1 was not here-wanted to know whether the previous section covered salmon or not.
I was here; but this section refers to canned foods.

This is the
same thing. Is the article salmon covered under the term "food or food products?"

I think that that
is very largely a technical objection.
[Mr. Motherwell. 1

It is no more
technical in one place, Mr. Chairman, than it is in the other.

Oh yes, I think a
real question was raised the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens).

The definition
we have here is the definition under which this act is going to be administered. Of course, I may be making a violent assumption in thinking so. There is your definition, that "canned foods" includes "foods that have been preheated, cooked, preserved," and so forth, and this very next section says "all canned fruit or vegetables, or products thereof"-there is no trouble about that- "or any food or food products which may be named by the Governor in Council," and so forth. It is perfectly clear that if in the opinion of the minister this section ought not to apply to fish it is no good our considering it now. Why not let the whole thing stand?
We might make a little progress, that is all.
I do not know that it makes a bit of difference letting it through while the other stands.

If we find the
interpretation clause has to be changed to exclude all kinds of fish, we can attend to it.
If you make the change in the first section it will have the effect of taking it out of this other section; there is' no question about that.

If we except fish,

My hon. friend is quite right; that is how it should be, but it is not so drawn. It is another evidence of the careless way in which these amendments are drafted. Mr. MOTHERW'ELL: I do not think it does either, but I should like to have the opinion of the committee as to the principle of selling the contents by weight rather than by measure.
I think every, one would say that that is right.

Chairman, I move that the committee report progress and ask leave to sit again.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. LOW (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no
change in this vote, which is for the purpose set out in the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, this item is of very much more importance than is indicated by the amount voted, although that is considerable. It deals with a subject which I know commands the interest and consideration of a very large number of the citizens of this country, particularly those engaged in educational and industrial affairs.
Parliament has from time to time given consideration to this matter; in 1918 or 1919 a very important committee of parliament studied it in considerable detail. It has been the view of many that the scope and usefulness of the research council should be extended and that their work should be recognized by larger support from the country. So far as I have been able to learn, the work they are carrying on is deserving of the highest commendation. Unfortunately I do not think the people generally either adequately appreciate the value of that work or are sufficiently acquainted with what is being accomplished, and parliament might very well spend an hour or two in the consideration of the activities of this very important branch of the public service. For myself I would like to see every member of the House become fully seized of the necessity and value of this work. As to the personnel of the council, presided over, I believe, by Dr. Tory, I think it is deserving of recognition; at least the efforts of the council deserve such recognition as parliament can give by a consideration of the work undertaken, the results accomplished, and the researches in prospect. Personally I would like to have seen the vote increased. I would like to see this type of work seriously taken up by parliament and the great educational institutions of the country, with a co-ordination of all activities to bring about the best possible results.
There is, for instance, the great question * of the natural resources of Canada, to which I know the research council have given a great deal of study and in regard to which they have compiled some exceedingly valuable information-information which, if parliament were fully siezed of its importance, would have a great influence upon its decisions in various lines as regards bills presented, estimates passed, and so forth. I would ask the minister to give the committee an outline of the work of this important body.

I agree with the hon. member that the work being carried on by the research council is of great value to all classes of industry. It is carrying on a number of important investigations; I might give the committee some idea of the work by citing

That is an interesting index, but it is not a very full or satisfactory description. May I ask the minister a few questions based upon the list he gave? He referred to matters affecting various phases of agriculture, such as soil bacteria, the question of rust, of winter hardiness in crop plants, such as clover, and so forth; tuberculosis in animals, and some investigations regarding grains, onion maggots, and wireworms. These are subjects directly connected with agriculture. Does the Department of Agriculture cooperate with the research council in this work, or is there duplication? We had a very lengthy dissertation of about an hour the other day on the part of the Minister of Agriculture on the subject of rust, in which, I must say, he displayed a good deal of personal insight into the question. Is the

information he gave in that connection based on the researches of this body, or are the two bodies, the research council and the Department of Agriculture, carrying on separate investigations into the same subjects? We ought to bring all these investigations on each subject under one control so that there will be no waste of public money. It would be better, for instance, for the research council not to touch a question at all if another department is spending a considerable sum of money on the, same line of research. That query is applicable not only to such matters as have been referred to, but also, for instance, to the fisheries. For example there is the sturgeon fishery, and other fishery ressources-are these being investigated by the officers of the Fisheries branch as well as by the industrial research council?

lam unable to speak authoritatively as to that, but I do know that each department co-operates to t)he very fullest extent with the research council. Whether in the particular instance my hon. friend refers to the investigation has been conducted separately by the research council, or jointly by the council and the department. I am unable to say. I understand that a very complete report on all these items has been placed in the hands of my hon. friend, and I have no doubt he has read it.

I rather regret the
minister's suggestion that my questions to him are influenced by a desire to indulge in captious criticism.
Not at all.

I am not influenced by
any such desire. I am deeply and honestly interested in the subject; I desire to support it and I want to see the vote passed. I should like to see this work enlarged, but I think it is due to parliament that we should have a very complete outline of what is being accomplished. I also think it is due to the industrial research council to have that done. As I have already stated I do not think their work is half appreciated by parliament owing to a lack of complete information as to what they are doing,

speechtext:
As one who, like my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) is deeply interested in research work and who has had some opportunity to see the advantages obtained by the co-ordination of effort along this line I think I can assure my hon. friend that the desired co-ordination is going on just as rapidly as possible. I do not think the Department of Agriculture, and the officers

Supply-Trade and Commerce
of that department, should be robbed of any credit due to them with respect to their investigations into tuberculosis; but as my hon. friend will admit a solution of the evil of tuberculosis is, perhaps some distance away yet. The bringing together of the activities of the research council and of the officers of the Department of Agriculture and the Mines branch is with the idea of effecting co-ordination ; and at the moment I can assure my hon. friend the work is going on in a coordinated way. My hon. friend will also admit that our universities should be given a great deal of credit for what has been accomplished in the past. They have inaugurated research work in a great many directions but in each case the investigators worked along particular lines, and possibly there may have been some overlapping in Toronto as compared with the work carried on in the universities of Alberta, or British Columbia. The effort of the research council is to interest scientifically trained men from one end of the Dominion to the other in these investigations, and they are succeeding in that object. Not only that but, they are also bringing about co-ordinated effort in those departments of the federal government where work of a scientific character is in progress also. This is a matter in which I have been chiefly interested myself, and I agree with my hon friend (Mr. Stevens) as to the necessity for co-ordinated effort along such lines. With respect to the results so far achieved one needs only to mention the discovery of marquis wheat which has been so frequently referred to in this House. No one can over-estimate the importance to Canada of the introduction of this particular variety of wheat. Nor can one over-estimate the value-whether we consider human beings or the animal kingdom merely,-of the discovery of a cure for tuberculosis. It is only by continued experimentation, and by thoroughly exploring every avenue which offers a possibility of success, that such a desirable end can be accomplished. Of course there are difficulties in the way of securing co-ordination on the part of all those interested. Nevertheless we are succeeding, and we hope to accomplish even greater results in this direction. The Mellon institute in the United States is an admirable illustration of what can be accomplished for example, by private enterprise. It seems to me that so far as the government of Canada is concerned no opportunity should be left to encourage the work of scientific and industrial research of, and through the money voted annually by parliament provide such facilities as will
enlist the co-operation of the best scientific minds available. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that we know far too little about, and that we appreciate insufficiently, the tremendous value to humanity and to industry likely to result from work of this character when properly carried on.

While this vote appears not
to be reduced, in reality it is, inasmuch as I understand it is the intention of the government to have this appropriation furnish the money for the assistance previously given to the Standardization Association of Canada, as I think it is called. I understand that the vote under that heading has now been withdrawn, and the association in future will either have to obtain funds under this particular vote or else will have to cease its activities altogether. Should this prove to be the case I think it is a matter very much to be regretted. When the House opened I placed a resolution on the order paper dealing with this question and although it is not likely to be reached now the subject it deals with is worthy of great attention. Perhaps I may be permitted to read the resolution in question as expressing briefly my views of the matter. It would almost look as if I had taken this step as a result of being prompted by the officials of that particular association because they found their vote had been cut off and consequently were appealing to members of parliament to give them some backing. I can assure the government, however, that I never heard of the association until I had placed my resolution on the order paper. I was prompted, to do so by seeing the measures Australia is adopting in this regard. I have not got my notes on the subject here, but if I recall rightly they were spending a large sum of money-if I am not wrong in the neighbourhood of S50.000-on the improvement and development of this branch of work. They realize apparently that it is going to be a very great thing for the industrial life of every country, and especially of every country that takes it up quickly. They have gone ahead on that line also in the United States, and as my resolution suggests it resulted in the saving of millions of money to the United States government and that only in its capacity as a purchaser because it was enabled to buy so much cheaper by standardizing its requirements. If the committee will allow me I will just read my resolution through. It is as follows:
Whereas, standardization in engineering, manufacturing. and other allied activities is becoming increasingly necessary in order to stop the huge economic loss

Supply-Trade and Commerce
now occurring, and the subject is now engaging the attention of all the leading nations of the world.
And whereas, those countries which are advanced in national industrial standardization will have established a great commercial ascendancy over those that are not so organized.
And whereas, the progress already made in this direction in the United States has resulted in the saving of millions annually to the United States government alone in its capacity as a purchaser.
And whereas, some of the advantages of standardization are:-
Makes mass production possible.
Stabilizes production and employment.
Eliminates indecision in production.
Stimulates research and development as to the best types, and encourages the adoption of the best standards.
Helps to eliminate practices which are merely the result of accident or tradition and which impede development.
Provides a truly competitive market in which to buy material and equipment, giving accurate definitions to enable the purchaser to know what he is buying and whether he is getting what he bargained for.
Makes it easier to repair and replace equipment.
Reduces the cost of manufacture.
Simplifies the keeping of cost accounts.
Increases the production and efficiency of industry.
Will go far to eliminate disputes and litigation as to whether the product is in accord wtih the sample.
Or, otherwise expressed, standardization means to the producer increased production, better quality at reduced cost, and to the consumer a better article for less money.
Therefore, this House is of the opinion that the' government should be asked to investigate and encourage the development of standardization in Canada.
I was not aware at that time that we had any association handling it, and I would earnestly urge the minister to consider the possibility of giving, in the supplementary estimates this session, sufficient money to carry on these activities. At present they have only a small grant. I think it is a retrograde step to do away with their investigations, and if you place the expense upon this vote now under consideration, it just means that some other necessary investigation has to go without sufficient funds. I submit the Minister of Trade and Commerce might well consider whether he could not see his way to give assistance to this very necessary work.

It is true as my hon. friend says that the vote for $10,000 included in last year's estimates has been dropped this year. This work will be earned on by the research council, and I will be very glad to take into consideration the recommendation of the hon. member that possibly an amount might be placed in the supplementary estimates.

The amount voted was $10,000.

I should like to offer my endorsation, for what it is worth, of the expenditure of money on scientific and industrial research in this country. It is one of the subjects we should all be interested in, because every industrial country in the world to-day is going into it to a greater degree than we are. Before the war Germany made many of her advances because of the high type of research in which she took part. There are in the northern section of Ontario two subjects upon which research will undoubtedly bring a great deal of value. I do not know that they are subjects-one of them at least is not-which the government should deal with; but at any rate any subject which would mean wealth to the country might be well considered by the government or by its staff of officers. The first subject I was thinking of-and I believe that a certain amount of work is now being done with regard to it in the Mines branch-is in regard to discovering some method by which the types of iron ore in Canada can be used economically. I know there has been a certain amount of work done in this matter, and if Canada could develop some method by which the magnetite ores in Canada-which are not of such a high grade as in the United States- could be developed, then Canada would have the greatest iron resources of any country in the world, because we have scattered all over the country hundreds of millions of tons of ore. So far, outside of the Helen mines, there have not been discoveries made of the hematite and the other types of ore which are most useful, but if we can discover some method, either by electric smelting-and we have great electrical possibilities in the northern country-or some other means of utilizing these magnetites in some portions of Canada, it would be of great value to the country. There is another subject-and this is the one which perhaps the government might say it was not their duty to deal with-and that is the question of pulp and paper. I remember on one occasion, speaking to Professor Ma-callum, who was chairman of the Industrial Research Commission, and he informed me- and the statement was concurred in by prominent men in the pulp and paper industry-that at the present time in that industry there are very valuable products which have been allowed to go to waste out of which great value will ultimately be taken. I do not know if I could go into an analysis of the subject, but he made the statement to me before a prominent pulp and paper man. who admitted it was correct, that that industry was merely in its infancy. I believe

those subjects are of such importance-and there are many others in Canada perhaps of like importance-that they might well be made the subject for research by the Dominion, even if ultimately the profits which came from those investigations go into the hands of private individuals; at least it would mean the development of the Dominion of Canada. I wish to endorse all that can be said in favour of this development in Canada at the present time, so long as the government sees its way clear to spend money to carry on this work. Utilization of Canadian low grade iron ores.

We have a special laboratory dealing with the pulp and paper problem, and the work is being co-ordinated with the work of the scientific research council. What we have been endeavouring to do there is to utilize the jackpine, for example, which carries a large percentage of pitch, by working out the problem of elimination of the pitch and making the product useful for the manufacture of pulp and paper. So much has this appealed to the pulp and paper manufacturers that they are voting us this year $20,000 to assist us in this work. As regards the diseases of trees, work of this character has been carried on in the eastern provinces. But again we have it in the different departments. What I tried to impress upon the committee was that the endeavour was to co-ordinate the efforts being made in regard to all these different problems because, as a layman, it seems to me, if we are going to get results, the thing to do is to bring the scientific men in council together to discuss these problems. The chemist may be dealing with the problem of iron, and he may supply the missing link that the man working on forestry has missed, because he is a scientifically trained man. That is why it is important to get the work co-ordinated by bringing the men together to discuss these problems. In that way we are going to receive value for the money invested and reap the greatest advantage.

From an examination, during the brief time it has been in my hands, of the report the minister so kindly sent over to me, it is apparent that the question of the utilization of ores has oeen solved. Take, for instance, the first contusion of the committee. It reads:
The building up of an iron mining industry in Canada in the near future can be accomplished at a reasonable cost.
There are large deposits of iron ore in Canada which under present conditions are lying idle because the ore cannot be profitably marketed, but which can be utilized to supply central Canada with iron ore if deemed advisable.
The desirability of establishing an iron mining industry in Canada should be impressed upon the government.
The most promising method of utilizing Canadian ores is to prepare them by beneficiation, if not naturally suited, for treatment in blast furnaces by the present blast furnace process.
Special processes, including electric smelting, which have been devised to treat iron ores, are not under present conditions likely to be a big factor in building up the industry in Canada.
During recent years good progress has been made in methods of beneficiating iron ores, prior to reduction by the blast furnace process, and these methods are applicable to Canadian ores.
I have had a chance only of glancing at this report, and my hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong, but it would appear that this ore can be commercially turned to immediate account, and that in order to get it turned to immediate account steps have to

be taken by the government. Take, for example, recommendation 12:
A bounty of fifty or seventy cents per ton of merchantable ore or concentrate would encourage operators to proceed with attempts to utilize Canadian iron ore. This bounty would be insufficient to warrant expectation of immediate profits from operation of the known deposits, but would perhaps be sufficient to warrant the operation of some mines now idle and the installation of plants for sintering the ores, and the carrying on of further large scale investigation which must be at least partly paid for from proceeds of the sale of iron ore and concentrates.
The great desirability of this being done in the interests of our railways is also pointed out, also the earnings we would make out of it. Then, of course, there would be a saving on account of our not having to buy so much ore, as we now do, from the United States. I observe that we have a direct recommendation in that respect. In the preface the committee say:
The committee believes that if a small bounty of say fifty cents a ton was paid on the beneficiated Canadian ore, or any natural ore of equal grade and quality which might be discovered in Canada, for a period of about ten years, this would go far tc even up the price difference-
That is, the price difference between this ore and the cheap American ore.

For instance after weighing in and out at Port Arthur and Fort William it has been found on many occasions that as much as 50,000, perhaps 100,000 bushels have been left in the government elevator in days gone by. Of course from time to time all elevators have surpluses, more or less, at the end of the year when they weigh up. That is a well known fact.
It is the practice then to give the farmers the worst of it when their grain goes into the elevator and to give the elevator the best of it when the grain comes out?
Those are the overages which are referred to in the report of the Royal Grain Commission. A case was decided a few days ago before the Supreme court in reference to that very same matter.

Is there any provision
for inspecting the weight of coal in car load lots? My reason for asking the question is that I have received a number of complaints from coal dealers that it is practically impossible for them to get the full weight that they pay for when they buy the coal in car load lots, and they are unable to get any

Supply-Trade and Commerce
adjustment because if they make any complaint they are not supplied with coal the next time they need it. Therefore in order to get regular supplies of coal they have to accept a continual shortage and either take the loss themselves or pass it on to the consumer. Is there any provision for the inspection of car load lots, and will the minister look into these complaints?

I may say that at the moment
the Board of Railway Commissioners are now investigating complaints of shortages of ooal in car load lots.

Will the minister say
that he ever read that $200,000 report of Mr. Justice Turgeon and his associates?
I have read a large portion of it.

It seems to have passed
out of the minister's mind very rapidly. What I cannot understand is this: Here is a report -the most expensive report this country was ever called upon to pay for-and one of its chief findings is these frauds in respect to grain elevators and it finds ten or a dozen. The minister says "We have prosecuted all brought to our attention," and then his deputy says "that all that were prosecuted were six," and he does not know who the six were. On the other hand the royal commission finds that of the twelve cases they discovered only two offenders were prosecuted. These statements do not agree. Which is right?

That may be in a period of
two or three years.
Surely a report that cost that amount of money cannot be wrong.

Will my right hon. friend say
that the twelve oases referred to were in the one year? My deputy informs me there were six or eight last year.

That has nothing to do
with it. The revelation was last year. I presume the offences extend over many years but prosecutions take place at the time of the revelation. Now, where are the prosecutions following the revelation?

The department has been
prosecuting every year.

Then the report is
wrong.

I have not the paragraph in
the Royal Grain Commission's report to which my right hon. friend refers 'before me.
The deputy will remember it. Surely some one in the department has a digest in his mind of this report. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre will be more detailed.

We must enlighten the
minister a little I think in regard to this. If the Chairman will give me a moment I will locate that part of the report where 9 p.m. the matter is dealt with; the report covers quite a large field.
I do not want to read too much; I think I have the matter here:
In the case in question a former agent of one of the companies-
I am reading from the Royal Grain Commission's report, page 26-
-told us that in the year 1921 he tampered with his elevator scales-
This individual said himself he tampered with these elevator scales-
-by filing a notch in the shoulder of the beam behind the zero mark in such a manner that the poise could be pushed back of this zero mark-
What year was this?
This is in 1921. Certainly 1921 is not this year; but let the minister dismiss from his mind whether it was this year, last year or the year before.

What I want to know is
whether the offences cover one year, two years or three years?
If the minister will follow the matter through he will get the whole story. Simply to say that because it was in 1921 it is a long time ago-

That is not the point at all.
I would like to know in what years the twelve offences referred to in the report were committed?

I am going to read this
again:
In the case in question a former agent of one of the companies told us that in the year 1921 he tampered with his elevator scales by filing a notch in the shoulder of the beam behind the zero mark in such a manner that the poise could be pushed back to this zero mark and thus cause the scales to register false weight, and that he used the scales falsely adjusted in this manner during part of the season. He alleged that he performed this manipulation on the instructions of the travelling superintendent of the company. This superintendent gave evidence denying the allegation in so far as he was concerned and disclaiming all knowledge of the illegal filing. It also appeared that this superintendent had dismissed this agent from the company's services on the grounds of incompetence and carelessness. Giving due weight to all the evidence adduced in this case, and which it is unnecessary for our purposes to review here, we cannot hold the superintendent guilty personally of the charge made against him but

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the scales were in fact found to have been tampered with in the manner described by the agent. The company has since removed this damaged scale beam and put in a new one. Under the rulings which have been given so far on this question the mere having for use in one's possession of scales in this condition, even without knowledge, is an offence under the provisions of the Weights and Measures Act rendering the defective beam liable to seizure and the owner to the penalty of a fine. This means that it is the duty of those who deal with the public in the buying and selling of merchandise to make sure that they have not in their possession and use scales which have been falsified.
In other words, it throws the onus upon the person who owns the scales.
We reported this case to the Department of Trade and Commerce recommending that it be followed up and that steps be taken by inspection to ascertain to what extent, if at all, the practice of tampering with elevator scales is being carried on.
I pause there to suggest to the minister now that the $200,000 royal commission has brought it to his attention, is it not extraordinary that he has not the information before him or in his mind? That is the point we are complaining of. Then I proceed to read:
We were informed that upon several occasions in the past beams containing a false zero notch, such as the one described in the case heard by us, had been seized by inspectors of the Weights and Measures branch, Department of Trade and Commerce. Upon receiving the report of the case brought before us at Moose Jaw in August, 1923, the department took immediate action to discover what elevator scales showed signs of having been manipulated, and twelve seizures and prosecutions have since taken place. In each of the cases the tampering was of the same nature as that described at Moose Jaw. A notch had been filed in the beam behind the zero notch so as to provide for the registering of an incorrect weight, the difference thus created in favour of the buyer ranging, in these eleven cases, all the way from thirty to a hundred pounds.
That is, thirty pounds in a wagon load, not in a car.
The wagon load is first weighed correctly, the poise being set at zero and a true weight given. Then after the grain is unloaded the poise is slipped back to the false notch, and the extra weight thus created is added to the weight of the empty wagon, thus increasing the deduction to be made from the gross to give the farmer the net weight of his grain.
Then the report continued:
In eleven of the twelve cases convictions were secured. In all these cases, however, nothing further was proved than that the companies had possession of the scales and were using them.
This is the point.
In each case the agents denied having used the false notch on any occasion. Some of them stated that they were unaware of the existence of the notch until it was pointed out to them by the inspectors. Others said they had found it on the beam when they took charge of the house. The superintendents of the companies likewise disclaimed all guilty knowledge of the condition of the scales. In some cases the company m possession had taken over the elevator only recently frorn a company now out of business, and the false notch might have been there prior to the change of ownership. Again the manipulation might have been 
the work of a guilty agent making a profit for his own purposes. Many explanations, of course, are possible besides that of guilt attributable to the company itself. It is worthy of note that these twelve cases affect ten different companies, one company being found to have two such scales in its possession the others only one each.
Which I referred to a moment ago.
Is my hon. friend not satisfied with eleven convictions out of twelve offences?

I am not and I will tell my hon. friend why. These convictions were merely formal convictions of a company having [DOT]in possession a scale with a notch in it, the company having disclaimed all responsibility, each individual in the company disclaiming responsibility, and there the matter stands. What I am saying to the minister is this: The offence is of such a contemptible and vicious character that it warrants the government following it up until it discovers who put the notches in the scale, and I think it could be discovered. I do not say it could be discovered by simply examining those who were involved, or taking their word. These commissioners, it will be remembered, were sitting simply as investigators of the grain trade. They were not investigating this specific thing and just happened to run across it. Naturally you could not expect them to put persons? on trial, but it was brought to the attention of the department.
My hon. friend says they were convicted.
I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the convictions under the act simply meant that the company was convicted of having in its possession scales that were false.
The law gets after the owner of the scales; but, is there nothing in the act by which the man perpetrating the fraud can be convicted?

I have not the act before me and cannot quote the section. Certainly anyone who is guilty of perpetrating a fraud under the Criminal Code can be prosecuted.
I do not want to appear to over-emphasize this matter but it is a case of deliberate and vicious fraud.
I should like to correct a statement I made a few minutes ago. The deputy said he thought there were six or eight prosecutions last year. The correct number is fourteen.

That takes in prosecutions everywhere. I am trying to get the government and the minister to appreciate the desir-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ability of hunting down these criminals, not the companies themselves, not punishing the companies for having the scales in their possession and disclaiming responsibility, but to ascertain who are the individuals responsible and to prosecute them.

A matter has been brought to my attention just recently, and if I am not in order in discussing it under this item then I will stand corrected. I have been informed that millers throughout Ontario who purchase wheat, say at points like Goderich, find that there is a systematic steal. One miller informed me that out of some forty cars milled last year, every 1,200 bushel car was an average of eight bushels short, and every 1,500 bushel car was an average of eleven bushels short. I am not sure that that is a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce. It may be a matter for the grain commission, but if this systematic stealing has been going on as one miller put it, I think someone should look into the matter.
Item agreed to.

I would like to revert to item 372:
Printing of parliamentary and departmental publications, including cost of Canada Year Book, $90,000.
The right hon. leader of the opposition asked if the Canada Year Book had been printed at the bureau. The information I have now is that it has been printed there for the last four years.. About 1,500 to 2,000 copies are sold at $1 each.
Will the minister give us the total of this vote, not only the items of the cost of the Canada Year Book, but the balance of the vote?

There is an item of $22,000 for publications likely to be published in 1925-1926. I might give a detailed list:
Census:
Bulletins: We hope to have all bulletins out before April 1, but it would be well to allow, say $1,000 in case of failure.	[DOT]
Reports of 1921 census:
Vol. Ill: Families, dwellings, ownership of homes, rentals, earnings.
Has the minister in those statistics any estimate of the cost of grain production per bushel or per acre in the west? If he has, what is that cost?
I have no doubt that is given in some of the reports of the Dominion Statistician who issues a monthly bulletin. If my hon. friend will look through them, no doubt he will find them.

If the minister has three or four years to spare, I would suggest that he do it. I will undertake that at the end of that time he will not have found it, and I never had charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I notice the minister included in this item of $90,000 an item for agricultural statistics of various kinds. A few nights ago we were passing agricultural estimates, included in which were seiveral votes for printing. Are statistics, bulletins and reports issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and also by the Department of Agriculture on similar topics?
Mr. L0WT:	We are endeavouring to
eliminate all duplication. I do not think the same statistics are issued in the Department of Agriculture as in the bureau.

I think there was a vote for printing for the Bureau of Statistics the other night in addition to this.

I do not think so.
I am sure of it. I think the minister will find there was a very considerable vote for printing under the heading of Bureau of Statistics.
There may have been sotnething under the item of the census.

Why is all the government printing not estimated for together and the detailed items given instead of being scattered around in this way? This, of course, is a mere fraction of what government printing is costing. Does this always appear in the estimates by departments? Are there not Printing Bureau estimates by themselves?
Yes. I am sure my right hon. friend, who has been in this House for so many years, realizes that each department has its own expenditure in connection with these items.
Does the vote for "Dominion Bureau Statistics, including western census," cover printing?
That covers the cost of the census and its publication.
It includes them, but there must be something else.

What is the cost of printing
the Canada Year Book?

What is the balance of $90,-
000 made up of?

I have just read a long list of
publications.
What is the system employed in arriving at the cost of production, say of manufactured goods of any kind?

Any information of that kind
is gathered in from the different manufacturers of a particular line, similar to the procedure with agriculture.
Does this include the cost to the Priming Bureau of distributing these parliamentary and departmental publications?

My right hon. friend
will find vote No. 264 for the distribution of parliamentary documents and other governmental publications, $40,000. That is carried in the Priming Bureau estimates.

What is the total bill for the printing of the Department of Trade and Commerce? There were sums under other items such as the Bureau of Statistics, In-

telligence service and so on. Under the i;em of public printing there are some items part of which no doubt come from the minister's department.

Why is it that the
salaries paid- in weights and measures inspection work do not appear under civil government?
They are all outside Ottawa.

Should they not be
brought into the serivce and placed under the Civil Service Act? We have 120 officers all over the country and there is no excuse now for leaving them outside; they are a permanent service, although they were temporary for a while.

They have been so treated for
years.

Item agreed to.
Relief supplies for the Leeward islanders, $7,500.

Are the Leeward
islanders the coal miners of Cape Breton?

Have the Leeward islands a governor of their own?
Yes.

He sent a cable to the Prime
Minister.

It came direct from the

He is merely the governor of
the island, not "governor general."

We supplied the building

They are British islands?

Why is it that our own native Canadians are discriminated against in favour of outsiders? If the Department of Trade and Commerce can give relief to the people of the Leeward islands why can this government not give relief to the Cape Breton islanders?

How much will it go
beyond that?

It will be below the engineer's
estimate.

That is, the contract
price.
Yes.

By the time the extras
are paid for what will it likely be?

The cost in connection with
the Edmonton elevator was I think within three or four thousand dollare of the estimate. I do not think there will be much greater difference in this case.

The same contractors are
building both.
Yes.

Has the contract been
let?

Who is the contractor
and what is the price of the contract?

has signed the agreement I would rather not give that information.
What is the name mentioned in the newspaper item to which the minister refers?

Did they build the Edmonton elevator?

Well, the minister has
already told us that the same contractors are building both, so that, he might as well oome out and tell us that the firm are Carter, Halls & Company, notwithstanding that the Governor General has not yet affixed his signature to the document. And at the same time we might as well have the whole story as to the price and so forth.

Was that not given in
the newspapers too? Does this estimate of $960,000 cover the superstructure as well as the preparatory work, the foundation?
This covers the elevator proper, not the foundation or the trackage.

The foundation has already been built under a separate contract. The minister therefore was safe in saying that the present contract for the superstructure would be below the engineer's estimate for the whole thing. What was the amount of the first contract for the foundation?

thing?
