I have an item given in an Ottawa despatch of May 19-the day I think the tenders were opened-stating that Carter, Halls & Aldinger, contractors of Winnipeg, were the lowest tenderers for the Prince Rupert government elevator at $865,000. How did such information get out when it was denied the House?
Is that from a Vancouver paper?

I presume it is.
Mr. LOW. Read the last portion of that despatch.
It says that the minister did not give it out.
Yes.

The minister gets the most extraordinary notions when one is asking a question of this character. I am not suggesting that the minister gave out the information. I am asking how it was given out when it was denied to members of the House.
That is easy.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) says it is easy. Well, I think he will agree with me that it is scarcely fair to members of the House that information should be denied us, and then the very day the tenders are opened it is printed in a paper on the other side of the Dominion.

This is my experience of the way it. is done. The representatives of the contractors are here, and as soon as the tenders are opened .each contractor knows what the other tendered for, and the discussion is then right out in the open. But that does not mean the contract is awarded, although an hour afterwards each contractor feels at liberty to tell everybody about it.

As to giving out the information, it would not be courteous on the part of the government to divulge the contents of an order in council until it has been completed by the signature of the Governor General, and until it is completed there is no actual contract.
The minister's explanation is a very good one.
It is the right one.

Possibly it is correct. But there is another aspect to this question which I think merits some attention. There are' those in the commercial world who are desirous to sell goods, we will say legitimately, to the successful tenderer, and they are very anxious to get information so they will have an opportunity of getting in touch with him. and so forth. Now, a very positive statement of this kind would indicate that the contractor did have some encouragement to believe that his tender was successful. That would place him or his friends, or those who were favoured with the information, in a position of advantage over those who were honestly awaiting the official announcement. The order in council was passed, I understand, on May 19, at least it was ready for passing on that date, and I do think it ought to be possible in a very important contract of this kind to announce the letting of the contract some time earlier than May 25. Once tenders are called for, if the government intend to go on with the work, they should publicly announce the granting of the contract as early as possible, so everyone interested may have a fair and even chance to sell his'goods for the work.

I can only say to my hon. friend that the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer, and the order was signed within two hours afterwards. As soon as it has been signed by the Governor General the announcement will be made.
What is the capacity of this elevator?
It is 1,350,000 bushels.
What will be the approximate total cost of the elevator without the trackage?

I have read out the full details as given to us by the engineer. The cost of the trackage, trestle and fill is $60,000, so if the hon. member will deduct that from the total amount he will have the balance.
The minister gave the total cost as $1,331,000.

No, $1,329,000.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I thought the figure he gave was $1,331,000 for this elevator. Can he tell us what the corresponding estimate is for the new elevator at Halifax?

The engineer's estimate was
$622,570. The contract has been awarded to E. G. M. Cape & Company, of Montreal, for $599,800.
That is to say, the government is putting in an elevator at Prince Rupert at more than twice the cost of the elevator at Halifax.

Not twice the capacity. The
Halifax elevator has a capacity of 1,032,000 * bushels.
But at twice the cost, I say. Is the 'minister aware that his colleagues, in order to win the by-election, promised a two million dollar elevator in 'the most definite terms?
They did not win the election.
That is the explanation. If it was not for the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) we would get very little frankness from the other side of the House.
Last year the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) said ithey did not need an elevator there.
The government estimate that it will cost $1,331,000 to elect 'their candidate for Prince Rupert.
That is wrong.
That is the way the member for George Etienne Cartier put it in his celebrated Winnipeg interview.
You haw to allow for accidents.

And a large allowance
must be made.

Mr. Chairman, when this matter was up initially last year I protested against the work, and I think I very fairly pointed out the traffic conditions at Prince Rupert. It would be such a good thing for this country if we could find some cheaper way for the government to look after its election expenses, some way in which a real benefit could be given to the people of Prince Rupert. Now we 'have this enormous expenditure of $1,329,000 for an elevator at a place where there is no business for it. Undoubtedly some of the government's friends 225
will make large profits in the supply of hardware, as they did in connection with the erection of .tihe warehouse there. This will help the gentlemen in the hardware business, but how does it help Prinqe Rupert? Again I ask, is there no cheaper way of doing it, if it must be done? Last session I asked what business there was to justify such an enormous expenditure, but I could not get any information. The government has now had in operation for some years an expensive warehouse at that point. There is one very distinctive thing about that warehouse-it is doing no business worth while talking about. Has the government ascertained what it is making out of its present facilities in Prince Rupert? It may be said that we cannot make money unless we have the facilities. Well, they have a great warehouse there, and they have a dock; what are they making out of it? The government never took the trouble to consider that aspect of it; a demand is made, the money is only the money of the taxpayer and it has to go. Surely the government will tell us what their estimate is of the business to be dope. Surely they will give us some reason why we should now throw away $1,329,000. They know what the loss is on the warehouse and they know what business is being done. They should give that information now.

Deducting the cost of
trackage, the total cost of the elevator will be $1,269,000. I understood the minister to say the capacity would be 1,350,000 bushels, so that it will cost approximately 94 cents per bushel capacity to 'build this elevator. Why is there such a great difference between the cost of the Halifax elevator and that of the Prince Rupert elevator so far as bushel capacity is concerned?
No doubt the conditions are very different as between Halifax and Prince Rupert-different as to foundation, trackage, and everything else.

I am afraid the minister must refer to political conditions. Last year when this matter was up we were told that an extremely favourable site was available at Prince Rupert on which to build this elevator. Beyond doubt there is not a better site on the western coast for the building of an elevator than at Prince Rupert, and if the figures were reversed and Prince Rupert were the cheaper point at which to build, there would be something in the minister's contention. As it is I think he should give us something further than the mere statement that the conditions are different.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Last year in discussing this Prince Rupert elevator I think it was the Minister of Railways who said that Prince Rupert was a better port for the Peace river country than Vancouver, or a nearer port. I wonder how soon we shall be able to use it; how soon we shall have direct rail connection from the Peace river country to Prince Rupert to justify the construction of this elevator.

This is an amazing situation. The ex-Minister of Finance criticizes the government for lack of information with regard to the estimated business to be done through this elevator after it is constructed. Every request for some information to justify the expenditure is declined, and not only declined, but no attention paid to it. The hon. member for West Edmonton gets up and asks the Minister of Railways if he will help to justify the construction of this elevator by building a line into the Peace river, but there is no answer from either minister in this connection. I am not opposing the construction of an elevator if there is need for it. I am not opposing the construction of this elevator if the promise of the Minister of Railways is carried out. If we get a line into the Peace river country there will be some justification for it.
My hon. friend will tell me, perhaps, when I made such a promise.
The minister allows the press to attribute all these promises to him and does not bother contradicting them.
I do not control the press, I regret to say.
He could contradict it very quickly.
I am too busy.

Working up ways of getting Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton together? If this government ever wishes to justify the construction of an elevator at Prince Rupert it will have to put its own line into the Peace river, for this reason: Any grain that is grown there at present, under terrible conditions, is shipped south over the Canadian Pacific to Calgary and goes direct to Vancouver, and unless the Canadian National makes direct connection with the Peace river country there will be so little grain going to Prince Rupert that there will be no justification for the construction of this elevator. If the minister cannot give the committee some better reason-indeed, some reason; he has not given any yet-for

this construction and also for the difference in expense to which the hon. member (Mr. Gardiner) has referred, I am afraid I for one cannot feel satisfied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no hesitation in justifying this expenditure. Prince Rupert is one day nearer the Orient than any other port on the Pacific. There is an opportunity for the handling at that port of a very considerable quantity of grain from the prairie provinces. I think the most important feature of the development will be the stimulation of agriculture in that large hinterland in northern British Columbia, which is an excellent agricultural country. I(t will make it possible for the farmer in that area to produce wheat on his land and find a market at Prince Rupert. To-day he is precluded from anything of that kind. If he produces wheat it must be sold locally. It cannot get on the world's market, because it cannot be transhipped back to Calgary or Edmonton and thence on the Canadian National to Vancouver. This elevator will do more to develop that great hinterland in northern British Columbia, which is tributary to what is known as the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, than anything else this government can do, and I have no hesitation in justifying and advising this expenditure.
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works could tell why this elevator at Prince Rupert is to cost twice as much per bushel capacity as the one at Halifax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot answer
my hon. friend's question. Unfair comparisons are very often made between the cost of elevator construction at Port Arthur and Montreal and the cost of similar construction on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and very often those who make such comparisons are not fully informed. Elevator construction in Vancouver harbour has been expensive and will continue to be so on account of the conditions in that harbour. At Prince Rupert I believe the same conditions exist. Earth filling had to be brought a considerable distance and dumped in in order to enable the piles to be driven for the foundation. These are conditions that do not apply to Fort William or Port Arthur. As to the other expenditures, I am not conversant with the contracts, though I know that tenders have been called and a number of contractors have tendered on the work. It should be remembered that in construction in the harbour of Montreal, for instance, you are dealing with fresh water where timber foundations will not be destroyed or affected by what is known as the toredo,

Supply-Trade and Commerce
which we have on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. The construction on the Pacific has been expensive, largely in connection with the foundation.

The minister told us a
little while ago that the cost of the foundation was $222,000. Well, once you have your foundation in, I should think the rest of the elevator could be built just as cheaply at Prince Rupert as at Halifax-cheaper, in fact. There is, however, a difference of half a million dollars in the cost, regardless altogether of the foundations.

There is a material difference in wage rates as between Prince Rupert and Halifax. The fair or current wage for a carpenter at Halifax is fixed at 57 cents an hour; that is the agreed rate between labour and the employers in Halifax. At Prince Rupert and Vancouver the rate will be approximately thirty cents an hour higher than that. The rate has not yet been fixed for Prince Rupert, but in Vancouver the rate is $7 for an eight hour day. The comparative rate for labour would he from 33 to 35 cents at Halifax as against, say, 45 cents in Prince Rupert. We have not yet definitely determined the rate that is to be paid, but the same comparison as between other classes of labour can be considered.

Would the
Minister of Labour tell us what the percentage for labour is in the cost of this structure?	.

No, I did not give this particular elevator construction any thought from that viewpoint. I am giving my hon. friend a comparison between the carpenter's wage which is about 30 cents an hour higher in Prince Rupert than it would be in Halifax. I should judge the labourer's wage would be about 15 cents, maybe only 13 cents, an hour higher, and the same holds good generally for other classes of labour, which would run up to a material item during the course of construction; I could not say exactly how much.

My hon. friend sees, of course, that we cannot get any very useful result in regard to this structure unless we know what the percentage of the labour cost would be. I understand this is to be a concrete elevator. Has my hon. friend ever considered the proportion of labour cost as against the cost of materials in concrete elevator construction? I should not think the carpenter work would be very heavy, but I may be wrong. My hon. friend is the expert on this question to whom I am appealing.
225i

There would be considerable carpentering work in concrete construction. There would be many form builders even in the construction of a concrete elevator, and all the concrete mixers and pourers would get a proportionately higher amount. I would say now-but this is only a snap shot opinion at the moment-that the cost of labour would be 30 per cent, possibly 32 per cent, higher in Prince Rupert than in Halifax, and I am judging from the carpenters' and labourers' rates which I have in mind.

I wish to deny entirely that this is in any sense a political elevator. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has referred to it in those terms, but I may remind the hon. member that in 1917 I carried that constituency by a majority of six hundred without any reference to construction of an elevator. In 1921, without the benefit of an elevator, I again carried the constituency, and I am sure that the same result will be once more achieved even without the aid of the elevator. However, Mr. Chairman I have spoken in this House on many occasions in support of this project. Therefore it is unnecessary, I think, for me to go into all the details again; to again refer to the fact that Prince Rupert is some 480 miles nearer the Orient than any other port on the Pacific; that there is a harbour there which is economical and easy of access-very little being required in the way of insurance, or pilotage charges. It is unnecessary for me again to go into all the details of these advantages. Our terminal rates are the same from Edmonton to Prince Rupert as they are from Edmonton to Vancouver. Our rates are also the same from Prince Rupert to Liverpool, or to any other port in Europe, as they are from any other port on the Pacific. I know that objection has been taken to this elevator, but the results will justify its construction. The hon. member for West York put his finger on the situation when he said the probable reason for building the elevator was that the railroad would require traffic. That is exactly the whole point. This country has a tremendous capital investment in the Grand Trunk Pacific. That railroad, known to-day as the Canadian National is no more unsound to-day than it was in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laufier. It was a sound project then; it is absolutely a sound project to-day. But if hon. gentlemen opposite continue their attempt to destroy this railroad it will never get anywhere. It is serving one of the best districts in the Dominion. If hon. gentlemen opposite will take the time to go
Supply-Trade and Commerce

out and tour that country they will find that the northern part of British Columbia is one of the very best districts in Canada. But the road can only be made to pay when traffic can be hauled over it, and you will find, Mr. Chairman, that this elevator in Prince Rupert will be one of the revenue producing assets of the Canadian National Railway.

If I really
thought that we would have traffic here and that any useful result would come from the building of this elevator I certainly would not object to it. My hon. friend tells me to go and visit the country. I have been up and down it, and I know a good deal about the costs of operating in that country. In certain directions it has much ahead of it; it has nothing ahead of it as a wheat raising country. It is simply idle and ridiculous nonsense to so describe it. I have been through that country and I know the cost of clearing land there. It is well wooded country that no one need be ashamed of. A district is not a bad district because you cannot grow grain in it at once so that it will pay. It is a good country but it is not a grain country. I know that there are places in it where the clearing of the land will cost $150 an acre, and in some places a far larger sum has been spent. Years ago I went through the accounts of one of the different colonization 10 p.m. projects that I had to look into, a town site proposition-I am now speaking from recollection which is pretty nearly right^and at that time the biggest crop that was raised along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific was town site propositions. Going into those accounts the cheapest clearing that I could find was at a place called Vander-hoof, where there is good soil and good agricultural possibilities; as I recollect it some forty-five miles west of Prince George. The clearing there cost-the trees were light, they were not the regular heavy British Columbia trees-only $35 an acre. In other words anyone that talks about raising grain in that country has got to start out with clearing h:s land at a cost of $35 an acre more than he can buy land for, that is land well adapted for grain raising, in a proper grain district. I still say that this scheme-you can only call it a scheme-is simply nothing else but another instance of political waste and political expenditure. Everybody knows that who knows anything at all about the matter. It is necessary that we should have traffic of course, but I should have thought that one of the things this government would want to do would be

to obtain traffic in a way that would pay the government system. What object is there, when the locality cannot and will not grow grain, to go into that country? They would lose money in doing so, and there are things in which they can make money, which they should go into. The grain comes from the prairie section to the east. What earthly use is there in this government turning round and making competition between their own terminals, Vancouver on the one side and Prince Rupert on the other? You have no grain in the latter district. You have to go east of that for your grain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will have
grain there.

Yes, possibly
you will, when the time comes that our vacant lands on the boundless prairies are taken up and you can get in your first crop; you will have some grain then. My hon. friend from Kootenay thinks they will have grain there. Well you can, if you go far enough. If you do that, you will have to carry your grain further. My hon. friend knows it and knows it well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Has my hon. friend heard of the Ootsa lake country?

We are getting
to a district that must be at least sixty miles south of the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; it is south of the line, but not that distance.

I would have
thought so. It is a first rate thing to spend money for something which may perchance happen, if not the next decade, the decade after, while we have got any amount of land and any amount of districts that are now ready to hand which are suitable; but the real truth is-and the minister knows it perfectly well-that if he goes back to where the grain is grown, where the movement is, he goes to a point so far east that it is just as easy to go to Vancouver as to Prince Rupert.
Is at not a fact that Vancouver is about 190 miles closer to Edmonton than is Prince Rupert?

I was about to give the figures. The mileage from Edmonton to Vancouver is 765.47, while the distance from Edmonton to Prince Rupert is 956. Of course if you are in the railway business for fun, and if you like deficits, carry your grain further than you need.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Is it not a fact that the
Canadian National Railways had to absorb the charge of $13 per car from Fort Mann in to the elevator at Vancouver?

I do not know
exactly how that situation is to-day, but I do know if they have to do that it is very easy for the government to put up their own elevator and their own terminals, where they have first rate water and save these millions.

May I
suggest to the ex-Minister of Finance that the hon. member for Skeena is evidently trying to mislead him? It is true that it costs $13 per car extra from Fort Mann to the elevator at Vancouver or approximately one cent a bushel, but we have to pay that, not the railway.

I think that
point is absolutely well taken. We have a cost now which is absolutely going to be a very serious thing. A question which has given the Minister of Railways a great deal of concern is the per mile cost of operation in Canada. Those costs now are so high that the system to-day, with railway freights that everyone is grumbling at, reports large deficits, and yet at a time like this we have an expenditure of $1,300,000, for what?-that so many more hundred miles of distance will have to be travelled at these high rates by this railway and its deficits multiplied. My hon. friend is in a great deal of difficulty in connection with it, and I sympathize with him in his difficulties in connection with the rate problem. I am only sorry that the government of which he is a member, and whioh he is bound to support, adds to the difficulties, multiplies charges and creates deficits by this sort of thing. What else can there be in it? There are the mileages. The mileages are 765.47 and 956, nearly 200 miles more, when every mile to-day is a most expensive operation. Why, to-day we had before the committee on Railways and Canals evidence to show that the cost of running a passenger car had risen to from 38 to 40 cents per mile. Of course the freight charges are less than that. There are more cars on the freight trains, but the upward trend is just the same. We have at present this situation; here we have an expenditure of $1,329,000, which, if it serves the purpose that its sponsors want it to serve, which if it carries grain, is simply going to add this much more to the present deficit by forcing the National Railways to carry that grain at the same rate just that much further and we had losses in this western territory of over $2,000,000 in the year when we had our
biggest grain crop. My hon. friend's own experts will tell him that if you carry grain at the present price over a given distance you absolutely lose money. Why, the grain rate used to be a paying rate, despite what the railways did say about the grain. It used to be a productive rate. It was low, it is true, but there was such volume, continuity and density that it paid. But if you get your underlying basis of expense up too high, remember that for every mile further you carry the goods you taper down your revenue, because you get to a point where, in connection with that tapering down, you are absolutely losing money for every extra mile you carry the goods. That is the situation here. Notwithstanding that situation this government of its own motion is going out of its way to add to the cost of the grain movement $2,000,000. Of course it will not do it. Hcxn. gentlemen are safe in that respect. That is what wouldl happen if the supposition on which all this is done were true, but it is not true. The grain elevator will not be used much more than the warehouse is used today. My hon. friend knows very very well the situation in connection with the warehouse. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways would not say the business in that warehouse to-day would justify its construction. There was one expensive thing to do. Having done that, having shown that the business was not there, in connection with commodities that that country can produce, it was the height of madness for the government to turn around and run into this expenditure in connection with such a thing as that country does not and will not produce.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) has referred to cheapness of construction on fresh water as compared with salt water, and he has also pointed out that the reason for that is that the toredo attacks the piles in salt water and does not do so in fresh water. That is something that we have been contending for a long time in New Westminster where the Fraser river has been coming into prominence from a shipping standopint in the last year or so. The Minister of Public Works knows all about the Fraser river; he knows about the available sites for elevators that we have there, sites that are already owned by the government or by the Canadian National Railways, sites at Port Mann, which have already been referred to, sites at New Westminster costing something like a million dollars, largely vacant at the present time, half a mile of water frontage at Woodward's landing 'a few miles below New Westminster. All
Supply-Trade and Commerce

of these sites are owned by this country or by the Canadian National Railways, which is the same thing. It has been stated that
this elevator is not a political one. Why is it that the Fraser river is being passed over and an elevator is being constructed at Prince Rupert? Where does the justification for that decision come in? It cannot be that men engaged in the grain 'business have recommended that the elevator be located at Prince Rupert in preference to the Fraser river. I do not believe you can get any grain expert who will say any such thing.
Another matter which has also been referred to and which has been pointed out from time to time to the Minister of Public Works and also to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) personally is that there is a loss to the Canadian National Railways in having to haul grain to Burrard inlet when it might be shipped from Port Mann or some of these other sites on the Fraser river. Something like $13 a car is being absorbed by the Canadian National Railways for all grain which is shipped past the Fraser river, the Fraser river is the first point where ships can come in and get that grain. This matter has been put up to the Minister of Public Works many times by the citizens of New Westminster and the surrounding district. It has also been put up to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If this is not a matter of political discrimination, what is it, and' why has the Fraser river been passed over in this way? The Minister of Public Works knows that one of the greatest authorities on grain elevators in Canada, Mr. Howe, has reported that the Fraser river is the proper place for the location of a government grain elevator.
Another matter to which I might refer is this. The Minister of Public Works will remember that when the citizens of New Westminster petitioned him and the government for the construction of a grain elevator at New Westminster, they were told that the government was going out of the grain elevator business; that the government was not going to construct any more elevators. Now we find the Prince Rupert elevator coming along. Why is that? I should like to have some_ reasonable explanation of the decision of the government to build this grain elevator at Prince Rupert rather than on the Fraser river, where the government owns sites and where it will be so much to the benefit of the Canadian National Railways to have elevator facilities.

There might be some justification for building an elevator on the *

Fraser river, but there is absolutely no reason for building one at Prince Rupert. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), in advocating the building of this elevator, says that it will develop trade along the Grand Trunk Pacific. If you do that, you take trade from the old Canadian Northern, which is the same thing. They all belong to the Canadian National. Wheat has to be hauled 200 miles further to get to Prince Rupert. The Minister of Public Works endeavoured to justify the building of this elevator by saying that a big hinterland will be developed in British Columbia. That is business that may not come for years and that may never come. We have been building railroads fifty years ahead of the times, and now the government is starting the same policy of building elevators ahead of the times. I would be the last one that would knock anything that would develop any port; in fact I am in favour of developing our ports; but I see no justification whatever for building this elevator at Prince Rupert. It is absolutely wasting the country's money to spend $1,300,000 at that point. If the government were spending their own money, they would not spend it in this way, and they should deal with the country's money just as they would deal with their own. I will not say this is a political elevator or anything of the kind, but it is an ill-advised expenditure. The government should wait until the country develops and an elevator is needed. There is no grain in British Columbia in the great hinterland the Minister of Public Works talks about, and he knows it will be a long time yet before grain is produced there to ship to an elevator at Prince Rupert.

I have no intention of opposing the building of an elevator at Prince Rupert, for I gave it my tentative support last year in the belief, of course, that it was to form part of a general development of that part of the country including the Peace river district. I shall, however, leave the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) to deal with that phase of the situation. I want to call attention to another phase which, I think, is of some importance. I might say, by the way, the proper time, if I had wished to oppose the building of an elevator at Prince Rupert, was last year when the expenditure was undertaken. I did not oppose it then and I do not intend to oppose it now. I wish to call attention to the cost of construction. Last year we were given an estimate, and on that estimate was largely based our decision and the vote we cast. I admit, of course, that was

Supply-Trade and Commerce
a very rough estimate as given, but it was given as an estimate on which the House might base its decision as to the wisdom of building the elevator. May I quote just a few sentences from Hansard of last year from the statement made by the then Minister of Trade of Commerce, the present Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), which gives to the House exactly the suggested conditions under which that elevator was to be built and the suggested cost:
Mr. Robb: I cannot state the exact cost until the plans have been drawn in their entirety. My hon. friend lives in a country where they build elevators. Ho knows that elevators are built so that they can be enlarged. I imagine that the capacity of this elevator is not to exceed 500,000 bushels. My hon. friend has probably prepared contracts and doubtless knows that the cost of an elevator depends primarily upon the expenditure involved in building the foundations, the cost of getting stone and cement. It is estimated that these elevators can be built at around forty cents a bushel. That is the yard stick you start out with.
May I interpose? The yard stick by which we measured the feasibility of the project when it was first mooted.
But the expenditure depends primarily on the cost of the foundations.
Sir Henry Drayton: Your foundations should be cheap in that locality.
Mr. Robb: I imagine so.
I am not accusing the then Minister of Trade and Commerce of deceiving the House, but I am pointing out that it is a most unfortunate thing that in this House we should be committed to large expenditures in the face of such vague estimates as these. I think we had reason to suppose that the estimated capacity would approximate the capacity of the elevator as constructed, and that the real cost would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of the estimated cost as then given to us. And that is the point I wish to bring to the attention of the committee. I emphasize it because this is not the first time that we have found ourselves committed to an expenditure far exceeding our expectations, an expenditure based on rough estimates given apparently without any foundation in knowledge or fact.	For my part I protest against
such things.	Had I known that the cost
would actually be double the cost given to us at that time, had I known that it was doubtful whether the Peace river country would be opened up in the near future- which one would suppose to be one of the chief justifications for the expenditure-my vote at that time would have been very different. I would impress upon the ministers of all departments that they owe it to this House as well as to their own reputation for accuracy in the future to be careful when they enter upon any new project to give to the
House some intelligent idea of the approximate magnitude of the undertaking as well as the approximate cost of it.

I have no intention of
criticizing the government for constructing an elevator at Prince Rupert, but I want to point out that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) suggests as a justification for the work the development of the hinterland, the northern part of British Columbia, with particular reference to the district around Ootsa lake-Francis lake, Nechaco valley, Bulkley valley and Vanderhoof. There are some excellent agricultural lands in the northern part of British Columbia, but I want to tell the Minister of Public Works and the government that had they built an elevator at Prince Rupert at one-half the present cost it would have served the purposes of the locality and could have been enlarged later on to meet any development in trade. Had they done that and taken the balance of the vote, of $600,000 or $700,000, and devoted it to some demonstration farms for the assistance of mixed agriculture in the northern part of the province, they would have advanced the interests of that section. The elevator, if its success warranted an extension, could easily have been enlarged. But what is the government doing now? It is wholly disregarding the dairying and mixed farming possibilities of that great northern section; and the one thing that northern British Columbia requires is the development of mixed farming, for this is its basic agricultural possibility, rather than the growing of grain. Some grain may be grown in one or two districts but not to any great extent, while undoubtedly there are large possibilities in the direction of mixed farming. I suggest to the Minister of Public Works that as the chief adviser of the government from the province of British Columbia he certainly has not done the northern part of that province a good turn by advising the government to spend $1,300,000 in a new elevator. The government could have provided first rate elevator facilities at a cost of $500,000, and the structure could easily have been extended next year if the circumstances made such an extension imperative. Instead of that we are committed to a contract for $1,300,000, which I think it will be admitted will be largely experimental.
A word now with reference to the suggestion made by the hon. member (Mr. Stork), that it costs $13 a car to haul grain from New Westminster to Vancouver. That is true; the Canadian National Railways have to pay for the service when moving grain over the line from New Westminster to Vancouver.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Furthermore, the New Westminster bridge has about reached its traffic capacity. I have no hesitation therefore m saying that the time is past when the government is warranted in longer delaying building on the Fraser river facilities for the export of grain from the terminals of the Canadian National. After many years of study of the whole problem, I do not hesitate for a moment to say that this expenditure on the Fraser river is more warranted1 than the expenditure of this $1,300,000. I do not want hon. gentlemen to go away with the impression that I am opposed to development at Prince Rupert; I want to see Prince Rupert developed and the harbour there utilized. I do say however that the Minister of Public Works has ill advised the government in neglecting the mixed farming possibilities of northern British Columbia while, so to speak, putting all his eggs in one basket.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh no.

That is what my hon.
friend has done. The government could have spent half a million on this elevator and provided first-class facilities for some years, adding to them as the grain trade developed; and the balance of the money could have been devoted to developing other branches of agriculture more suitable to the district than that of grain growing.

A little
while ago I said to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) that one of the reasons given for the construction of this elevator was the fact that there were great possibilities in the way of grain shipments frqm the Peace river country. The minister shook his head. Well, I should like to read from Hansard of last year what the minister had to say on this subject. At page 4318 he is reported as follows:
I know my hon. friend is not very friendly to the Prince Rupert scheme of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but so long as we oppose every proposition to give the Grand Trunk Pacific traffic, so long will the Grand Trunk Pacific give us a deficit. The Grand Trunk Pacific was not intended to be sawed off at both ends; the original scheme was to have a line of ships connecting at Prince Rupert with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental; and although conditions have somewhat changed, yet the fact stands, and cannot be controverted, that the route from eastern or from western Canada to the Orient via Prince Rupert is shorter than any other route by a good many miles. If we are to export our grain or other products by the shortest route at the lowest cost, Prince Rupert must be developed and utilized; there is no question about that. My hon. friend also forgets that there is a vast territory which, when opened up, will be tributary to Prince Rupert and will be many miles closer to Prince Rupert than to Vancouver. The grain shipments from the Peace river country to-day have to go around to Edmonton, which city is of course closer to

Vancouver than to Prince Rupert, but when that country is opened up, as it must be, it will be miles closer to Prince Rupert than to Vancouver by way of Edmonton.
Now, the Peace river country as a good grain growing district which is capable of producing millions of bushels of wheat of a high quality; and -the remarks which the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) made regarding the land along the Grand' Trunk Pacific certainly do not appl(y to the Peace river country.
You are right about that.

We shipped about 3,000,000 bushels in 1923, and altogether I do not believe that there is more than about ,one-tenth of the good grain growing land in the Peace river country which is under actual development. There are millions of acres of fertile grain growing land there that do not require any enormous expenditure to bring it under cultivation for the production of wheat. It seems to me that all the other arguments I have heard for this elevator are simply besidip the mark, and it was because I believed it was necessary to the Peace river country that I was in favour of voting this supply 'last session. The argument is advanced that Prince Rupert is four hundred miles nearer the Orient than Vancouver. Last year when arguments were brought forward regarding how far Prince Ruipent was from the Panama canal it was said: "Why, two hundred and fifty miles, and that distance on the sea does not amount to anything." But two hundred miles on land does amount to a great deal, and Prince Rupert being two hundred miles further away from the rest of the prairie country than Vancouver is, I do not think the grain traffic is going to move in any great volume in that direction until the Peace river country as tapped and made tributary to Prince Rupert, according to the statement of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) last session. I have mentioned this Peace River railway quite a number of times in the House this session, but it seems to me I am justified in again calling this to the attention of the government, for the reason that we are here voting money to build an elevator that apparently will be absolutely worthless, even for the railway, without the necessary branch line connection between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Peace river -country.

Mr. Chairman, we are faced to-night with an amazing situation. We have been- so faced1 on two or three occasions this session, and I notice by the estimates that we

Supply- Trade and Commerce
will be -treated to another huge anomaly one of these days. Here are we poor grain -growers in the west having an elevator forced upon us at Prince Rupert; another elevator -at Halifax forced upon us; the Welland ship canal, that will probably cost $125,000,000 to $150,000,000 before it is through, forced upon us, and' yet over a million people in the three prairie provinces have -been asking for the opening of the Hudson bay route for over thirty years without getting any consideration. What is the -matter? This looks to -me like the quintessence of gross discrimination, and I think the situation which is developing in th-is House will have to be -reckoned w-ith one of these days. This looks to me like another case of the Eequim&llt d-ry dock, forced upon ue for political considerations.
-Mr. OOOTE:	What about the Prince
Rupert dock?

That is another case of political expediency; while matters of real moment, matters that mean economic life and death to millions of our people, are passed over without any consideration whatever. I for one am certainly not satisfied to see this item pass.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I should think, Mr. Chairman, we might have got some reasonable explanation from the government, but any excuse they might make would have to be so lame, so pitiful and so halting that really I think they are adopting the course of wisdom in leaving the thing as it is. But there are just one or two considerations I am going to again draw to their attention. In the first instance, I entirely agree with the member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) that there is a first rate grain country in the Peace river district which may be served by Prince Rupert; it may never be. Undoubtedly the traffic from that district ought to be pulled in a westerly direction; there ought not to be a back haul east; but as to whether the line will come out in the neighbourhood of the Vermilion pass or not I do not know; if it comes out west of that pass I do not know exactly how far west it will come out, and even then I do not know whether it will come out so far west that the route will be cheaper than going to Vancouver. But in the meantime I am free to admit that there is a possibility that some day, when some policy has been evolved for the Peace river district, and when perhaps we have money to spend-because after all this thing relates to money, and even this government cannot
make political expenditures all over the whole map at once, and undoubtedly they remove the possibility of doing something in the Peace river country when they turn around and spend what they are spending here-but some day when perhaps we have money to spend this may be a better outlet for the Peace river district than Vancouver. We do not know. But we do know something about the conditions to-day, and I am just going to ask hon. gentlemen to turn up their Hansard at page 2059 of this session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman referring to a debate that has taken place this session?

No, Mr. Chairman, fortunately I am not; if I were I would be clearly out of order. I am referring to information which I succeeded in getting from the government in connection with this very matter, namely, the amount of business which is carried on in this territory.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I ask is it contained in a debate that has already taken place this session?

It is in the form of question and answer, and I have great pleasure in referring the Chairman to it. It will be found at page 2059 of this session's Hansard. I asked this question:
What are the respective freight tonnages moved by the Canadian National System on the line running from Yellowhead pass to Vancouver, and the line running from that pass to Prince Rupert in each of the years 1923 and 1924?
This is the answer given by the Minister
of Railways (Mr. Graham):	1923	1924Tons of revenue freight received at Prince Rupert from points east..	33,052	26,237Tons of revenue freight received at Vancouver	336,501	676,942In other words, the business to	Prince
Rupert in 1923 is less than one-tenth of the business to Vancouver, while, in 1924 the percentage is a great deal less than that. The whole thing is just simply a pity. It is a great pity that my hon. friends last session were misled by, to say the least, mistaken estimates. It is a great pity that with deficits as they are we are committed to the expenditure of $1,329,000 for an elevator that at present, whatever it may have in -the future, has absolutely no justification.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) is unduly alarmed. If he will just think back to the year previous to last year-if he
Supply-Trade and Commerce

was then paying any attention to the movement of grain through the port of Vancouver, as most of us were-he will very well remember that an embargo was placed upon western shipments, an embargo that was continued for several weeks. Why? Because the port of Vancouver could not absorb the grain coming down from the province of Alberta; and the comparison he is making now is proof positive of the necessity for some other outlet being provided. True, last year we did not have the crop in the province of Alberta that we had the year before, but I would point out to him that the same argument is being used now that was used against the construction of the elevator at Edmonton. In spite of the short grain crop in Alberta last year the Edmonton efevator has been full, and it has been full for the last two or three months, showing conclusively that it was good business to build that elevator there. It is true that there is not the traffic on the Grand Trunk Pacific line from Red water junction to Prince Rupert that there is over the old Canadian National line down to Vancouver, but that is because there are no facilities to take care of grain shipments to Prince Rupert. The construction of an elevator at Prince Rupert is warranted quite apart from the development of the Peace river country. It is warranted on the ground that it will provide traffic for the Grand Trunk Pacific line to Prince Rupert. More than that, it is a shorter route to the Orient, and are we not trying to develop trade to the Orient every day in the week, and to bring trade back from the Orient, and to do something for the railway line we have already built? I am quite in sympathy with the hon. member for West Edmonton in his desire to get railway facilities out of the Peace river country, and I have advocated it on every occasion. But, I say, quite apart altogether from that, the expenditure on the construction of this elevator is justifiable. If this year we are favoured with a crop such as we had two years ago I make the prediction now that the elevator at Prince Rupert will be full. So far as the cost of construction is concerned, I am not prepared to deal with that because I do not know the details. But I do know that a considerable number of contractors have bid for the work and where there is very strong competition the construction costs must have been kept within reason. As to the location of the elevator at Prince Rupert, it will be needed to take care of the grain trade of Alberta, and undoubtedly there will be grain grown in British Columbia in that large area north of and along the Grand Trunk Pacific line. True, 
it is not a paying proposition now, but if we do not provide facilities it never will be a paying proposition. When that Peace river country comes into its own and has an outlet, then not only the elevator at present proposed but perhaps another one at that point will be required.

I come from a section of the country where there are a great many elevators-the greatest elevator centre in the world is at the head of the lakes-and I have been listening to the discussion here to-night with a good deal of interest. At the same time I cannot help remembering that nearly all the elevators comprising the 65,000,000 bushel capacity at the head of the lakes were built by private capital. In other words, according to my experience-and it extends over many years at the head of the lakes- wherever grain elevators have been required for the business of the country, private capital has been only too happy to build them. Therefore it seems to me that if there was really a demand for an elevator at Prince Rupert private capital would have been ready to come forward for that purpose. There is no doubt that there is no line of business that has done so well as the grain handling business; I admit frankly that it has done very much better than the grain growing business. My hon. friends to my left will agree with me there, if they do not often agree with me in other respects. I do not wish to be put upon record as opposing the building of an elevator at Prince Rupert if it is needed, but I am making these observations after having listened to the discussion for some time. The argument that the elevator at Prince Rupert gives a closer route to the Orient by 400 miles is of very little importance. You can carry freight from New York to Calcutta at the same rate as from New York to Bombay, although there is a difference of 2,000 miles, and many other instances of the same kind could be given. Once a cargo is on a ship, a matter of a few hundred miles one way or the other makes no difference in the rate at which the cargo is carried. The Minister of the Interior stated that the eievator at Edmonton justified itself. I am not sure as to that. I do not wish to dispute his word, but I do know that some of the internal elevators, the ones at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw, are stated by the report of the grain commission to have been of no particular use. Certainly we might well have allowed private enterprise to meet any demand for an expenditure of this kind. At any rate the sensible attitude would appear to have

Supply-Trade and Commerce
been, to build at first a small elevator at Prince Rupert and see if it could get any trade. The idea of building an elevator of a capacity of 1,300,000 bushels at Prince Rupert and then carrying the grain 250 miles further-
My hon. friend knows that to build an elevator of a capacity of five or six hundred thousand bushels would cost within a hundred thousand dollars of an elevator with a capacity of a million bushels.

I hardly agree with that. Before the war the prices of elevators were graded according to the number of bushels storage capacity. I admit that a small elevator might cost a little more in proportion, but I should not think it would be anything like what my hon. friend suggests. So it might have been much wiser for the government to make the experiment by building a much smaller elevator, and then if very little traffic went through, there would not have been the same loss. However, I presume the vote will go through and1 I suppose it is our duty to make the best of it. But it seems to me in these times of heavy expenditure in all lines we might, well spend some of this money in the carrying out of better methods than those we are now following.
The argument of the Minister of the Interior is not very good. The grain that blocked Vancouver two years ago will not be hauled from that area to Prince Rupert in any case.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Part of it will.
Prince Rupert has been proved to be over 190 miles farther from that area than Vancouver now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that there is a portion of northern Alberta that is just as close to Prince Rupert as it is to Vancouver.

It is questionable whether the grain from the Peace river country will find its easiest outlet to Prince Rupert in any case. According to the minister's own statement, the first time there is a heavy crop in Alberta the result will be a block at Vancouver. I should say that Port Mann would be the natural place to build an elevator to serve the Peace river valley and that part of Alberta which has been referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand there is one under construction at Port Mann.

Why build this elevator away out of the reach of the grain route? It will be nothing but an expense on the grain trade and will add to the load carried by an already over-burdened industry. With regard to the elevators at. Saskatoon and Moose Jaw, I can state, I think with some authority, that when the Hudson Bay railway is built these two elevators will be used to their full capacity, but the Prince Rupert elevator will be nothing more than a white elephant for many years to come.

It was not my intention to say anything on this question, but now that the Peace river district has been brought into the discussion it may not be out of place for me to say a few words. I can remember when the elevator was built at Vancouver. It was not used for quite a length of time-in fact I have often heard people call it "Stevens' white elephant'- but that elevator has proven its worth.
Showing the foresight of the member.

It proved the foresight of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre in anticipating what ought to be done. If I were asked the question "Is the elevator at Prince Rupert before its time?" I would not want to say but that, perhaps, it is just a little previous. But when I look back at the effect the building of the elevator at Vancouver has had on that city I must say that I think Prince Rupert is entitled to consideration. Vancouver is not the only city on which the sun shines; there are other places entitled to elevators as well as Vancouver.
It has been said by one of the hon. members from Alberta that he has brought the Peace river district to the notice of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) a great number of times. I frankly admit that he has; but if the Minister of Railways would figure out the number of times I have called on him and advocated the opening up of the Peace river country I think he would admit that I have brought it up a good many times also. When I think of that vast empire up there in the northern portion of Britjsh Columbia I do not think any government is doing justice to the people of Canada as a whole in not giving that country an outlet; and I say that section of the Grand Trunk Pacific will never be on a paying basis until there is an outlet from the Peace river connecting up somewhere near Vanderhoof or Prince George. I have enough confidence in the Minister of Railways, to justify me in the belief that such an outlet will be built in the near future. An outlet ha3

been advocated for quite a number of years by way of Brule. I have always opposed that for the reason that the route from Brule to Grande Prairie would traverse barren country and a very expensive country to build a railway through, whereas the other route, for the greater part of the distance, would run through a good agricultural district. As to the cost of clearing the land in the Peace river country I heard one hon. gentleman say it would amount t,o $35 an acre. I would say that the cost of clearing land for the average homestead in the Peace river country would not be $2.50 an acre; in fact the greater part of the country is prairie land, with an amount of light timber on it. Taking all these matters into consideration, and recollecting what happened in the case of the Vancouver elevator, I think the government is justified in going on now with the construction of the elevator at Prince Rupert in that it has already been started.
Some little time ago I asked the minister the cost of the construction of the elevator leaving out the foundations. I think he looked it up and I should like to have the information.

Deducting the cost of the
foundation, which amounts to $222,000, and of the trackage, trestle and fill, $60,000, from the estimated cost of $1,329,000 it would leave $1,047,000. I notice that my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre has another question to ask.
I should like to ask the minister if it is intended to equip this elevator with patent car dumps, and if so what are they called?

The three elevator unloading tracks will have capacity for spotting fifty-four cars at one time on through trackage. The unloading facilities will consist of six track unloading pits equipped with power shovels, and two receiving legs.
There are not to be any car dumps?
Not at present, no.

I understood they were
provided for in the specifications.
No, I do not think car dumpers are provided for. However, I will look over the specifications.
I think we ought to know that. I understood it was provided for in the specifications. Surely the minister can tell me. There is a marked difference between these car dumps and power shovels.
No, there are no car dumpers.

Before the item passes I
should like to say that I am tempted by the remarks of the Minister of the Interior to point out that we are liable to have a congestion on the Pacific coast any year when we get a big crop in Alberta . Two years ago it only took two weeks to fill the elevators at several of the shipping points in southern Alberta, and then we could not ship any more grain to Vancouver. I think the Minister of the Interior is probably right when he says that a congestion of the elevators at Vancouver will make grain go to Prince Rupert. Personally I think it is following an unnatural route in going to Prince Rupert. However, all I want to say is this: I think it is very poor policy on the part of the government to construct this elevator at Prince Rupert before building one at Port Mann. I think the elevator at Port Mann would be used immediately it was completed and to its fullest capacity, because even during last winter we could not ship our grain to Vancouver without a permit, the elevators there being full to capacity most of the time. I think this shows what the country suffers through the old party system of government which seems to compel the government to build elevators, and other public works, for political instead of economic reasons.

When the item for the
building of the foundation of this elevator was under discussion last year I called the attention of the minister to the fact that in my opinion the structure would have no value until such time as an outlet was given from the Peace river district. I must confess that I supported the item last year, but I did so more or less on the general understanding that an outlet for the Peace river district would 'be provided within a reasonable period. I regret very much, Mr. Chairman, that we have no information before us at the present time that would lead us to believe that such an outlet will be given in the near future. I should like to support the remarks that have been made by more than one member to-night in reference to' the situation at Port Mann. I think if this elevator had been built it would have been of more advantage to the farmers of western Canada. On the other hand the elevator at Prince Rupert could have been built when it really was required. However, in view of the fact that the government has decided otherwise I must content myself by saying that I regret this money seems to me to have been wasted for the time being.

Canada and the West Indies and South America, or both service or services between, $340,668.66.

The contract has been renewed with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company until the 30th June, pending the conference which is to be held in the city of Ottawa. After that conference we will decide just what to do in connection with the subsidy.

I have in
mind the discussion which took place on this item last year, the year before and the year before that. It was pointed out to the minister then in charge that the boats under contract did not comply with the treaty regulations with the West Indies. They are old, out-of-date boats, some of them 'built over thirty-five years ago. They have whiskers on their joints and on their keels. Talk about the Canadian Government Merchant Marine; these boats are prehistoric dreams compared with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. They have not the speed requirements, the passenger accommodation, the tonnage, the warehouse facilities or the cold storage facilities required. They have not a single thing provided for in the treaty, and yet the government persists :in continuing the subsidies. Before this item is carried to-night, I would like the minister to give the committee some justification for the renewal of this subsidy to Pickf.ord & Black.

One of the most important
subjects to be discussed at the conference next June is the question of transportation, and until we have had that conference no change will be made in the service. There is no question that the boats that are in the service at the present time do not comply with the spirit of the contract, or the trade agreement made in 1920. After the conference we will 'be in a better position to decide upon a policy.

I wish to
reiterate my protest of previous years against the people of this country being asked to grant a subsidy to a privately owned, foreign steamship company, running in competition with our Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Is it any wonder we have deficits and difficulties? The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) who made a trip to the West Indies made a magnificent speech in the House this session in connection with trade and commerce. I desire to say that I am anxious to see our trade develop, and I absolutely agree with my hon. friend in the conclusion he arrived at, that if Canada wishes to develop trade in the West Indies we can
do it without spending a dollar on steamships, by simply taking down the trade barriers that exist between Canada and the West Indies, no matter what they do in that country. We do not grow articles in Canada which they grow down there, and we are not producing the things which they produce. Our manufacturers do not fear competition. Let us adopt the principle of reciprocal trade, if not free trade, and then it will not be necessary to subsidize privately owned steamship lines.

What is the reason for
paying this subsidy? Is it not because there is not sufficient traffic between the two countries?

I do not think it would be
possible to have this service without the subsidy.

Is there not a number of
merchant marine vessels plying on this trade now?

Two or three freight boats
but no passenger boats.
Are these mail packet boats specially fitted for passenger service?
Yes they are.
How long has this government been paying a subsidy to these boats?
Since the end of 1913.

Was there any subsidy paid
before that time to any line of boats?
Yes, it amounted to a little over
Could the minister tell the House the total cost to date of the subsidy in order to maintain this West India service?
About $5,000,000 in the last thirty years.

Will the minister give us the items which ,go to make up this $340,000, a list of the steamships that are receiving the subvention, Where they run and the period of
their service?

There are four steamers, and they Sail from St. John to Halifax, thence to Georgetown, British Guiana, every fourteen days, calling at the islands of Bermuda, St. Kitts, Antigua, Montserrat and Barbados, St. Vincent and Trinidad, and return from Georgetown to St. John, calling at ail the islands in the reverse order.

Four ships?
Yes.
What ships are they?
The Chignecto, the Chaleur, the Chaud'iere and the Teviot. The tonnages are: 4,744, 4,746, 4,019 and 3,270.
Gross tonnage?

No.
Are we then in default on that agreement?
We are, so far as this service is concerned.
Would it not be better to turn this subsidy over to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and use the merchant marine ships?
I do not think we Could use the boats as they are at present. It would require considerable expenditure on those boats to make them suitable for the service.

We have a number of Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships larger than these and some smaller tied up for three or four years. We have been paying a subsidy of $340,000 a year. We could have taken half of that subsidy and fitted up one or two of these ships at a time, put them into condition, then paid the balance of the subsidy and handed it back into our own treasury, instead of paying it out to these lines. It strikes me we should examine into the possibilities of utilizing the merchant marine ships on routes that we are now subsidizing, and the same argument applies to some of the other subventions to which we will come in a moment. I submit this to the government. I think it ought to ]?e carefully studied, not only studied but acted upon, and thus save to the country a considerable sum. In the first place, the minister states that we are not fulfilling the treaty or trade arrangement with the West Indies. I want to say, however, at this point, that the trade arrangement with the West Indies has resulted in a substantial increase in trade which I think is of value to Canada and justifies the making of the agreement. But we ought to try to discharge our obligations in regard thereto. I know the

minister has not listened to me, but what I have said I think is pertinent to the question, and I hope, although it is a vain hope, that he will read in Hansard to-morrow what I have said.
What will the cost be of fitting up some of the merchant marine freight boats for carrying passengers?

I have no idea, but at the
moment, they are not properly equipped.
One year's subsidy would nearly build a new ship.

The minister's last confession is an amazing one in view of the fact that as long ago as three years I asked for that very information, and we were put off with: "We will try to find it-out for the hon. member," and "I will make a note of it and give the hon. member the information later." But they never bother about it. It is the same old farce of party politics again.
Did the Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats gain or lose money on this route last year?

I have no information on that subject in the Department of Trade and Commerce. No doubt the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), if he were in his seat, would be able to tell the hon. member.
To what time will this vote carry this service? To June only?

To the end of June of this year. It is on the basis of a twelve months' contract, and the contract has been renewed only to the end of June. If the same service is to be performed, or if after the conference it is decided to change the service and a larger vote is required for that, we shall have to bring it down in the supplementary estimates. The matter will be decided at the conference.

Would it not be just as well to let this item stand until the conference is held? What is the use of passing this item now and the minister having to come back to the House again with a supplementary estimate for the fulfilment of this service?
I do not think it makes a great deal of difference. We may have to increase this vote.

With whom is this conference being held in June?

With all the West Indian representatives who are expected here on the 19th June.

I am alarmed at the threat of the minister, for I regard it as nothing but a threat that he will likely have to increase this item. I have pointed out the way in which he, in carrying out the pledge of his own party, can develop trade with the West Indies, and his own commissioner, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has made the same statement in this House this session. I have no doubt that I am absolutely within all bounds of reason in supporting the attitude of the hon. member for Cumberland. I shall oppose with all my strength any increase in the subsidy to a privately owned steamship line. Let us use our own boats. Let us fit them up if that is necessary. Let us subsidize our own merchant marine instead of subsidizing individuals to put on privately-owned, especially foreign-owned boats in competition with our own vessels.
What was the subsidy first paid to steamers between Canada and the West Indies?
I have not the amount of the first subsidy that was paid thirty years ago. I have only back to the year 1914, eleven years ago, when the subsidy was the same as it is at the present time.

Apparently the subsidy grows as the traffic grows. I understand the idea of giving these subsidies was to develop trade which in time would become self supporting. Evidently that is not the policy. In this case, the bigger the trade, the bigger the subsidy! What is the minister's estimate of the amount he will have to pay in subsidies if he subsidizes privately-owned ships which will be of a nature that they will fulfil our treaty obligations with the West Indies?

If thait is so, this seems to be almost as bad as the proposed Petersen .contract. It would amount to about $140,000 per ship per annum, as I understood the minister to say that there were four ships. I do not believe the people of Canada would stand for this subsidy if they really realized what was going on. I did not realize before the size of the subsidy we were paying for each ship that was on this service. According to the statement .made 'by the hon. member for Bow river (Mr. Garland), which the minister has
apparently not attempted to deny, the boats are not up-tordate boats, they are obsolete and not fitted for .the trade. I am very much opposed' to passing this item with the information we have at the present time.
This is an agreement entered into in 1920 and we are simply attempting to carry out its terms. The last offer we had for a service that would meet the requirements of that agreement was $535,000.

The agreement that the .minister speaks of now expires this June?
Mr, LOW:	The contract with the Royal
Mail Steam Packet Company is simply from year to year, but the trade agreement was for ten years.

When does the
present contract for this service expire?

At the end of June of this year.
M.r. WOODSWORTH:	No contract is
signed beyond June of this year?
No.

Do the Royal Mail
Steam Packet Company that get this subsidy submit statements to show the business and the losses annually?
They do.

This subsidy that is paid to them annually would be sufficient, according to statements that I have received and that appear authoritative, to build a ship of almost 7,000 tons. Vessels .on the route at present are of about 4,000 tone. It seems to be very foolish policy to continue paying a subsidy to private concerns -that are running in competition, to some extent at least, with our merchant .marine, when we might as well have Canada's ,own vessels in the trade, and it would appear to be about as cheap to build new vessels if that is necessary than to go on paying this steamship subsidy to other concerns.
Has the minister consulted with officials of the government -merchant marine las to how much it would cost to fit out some of the smaller merchant marine boats for -this trade?

That whole question will be discussed at the conference. We have not consulted the -merchant .marine as to fitting up any of the present vessels. I am not sure whether any -of them could be fitted up for passenger service.
