Has the government no
policy at all on this question? The thing is becoming more amazing as we go on. The question of subsidies has been under discussion in this House during the last four years and in previous sessions we have had discussions similar to that which has taken place to-night. Surely the government must have realized that the point would be reached some day when they would have to face the matter more squarely than they have done in the past. The minister must have some policy up his sleeve.

In 1920, an agreement was
entered into with the West Indies whereby we undertook to perform certain services. In the meantime we must at least attempt to carry out our part of it.

The terms of the treaty have never been complied1 with by either the West Indies or Canada. Canada has not supplied the necessary service, and the Leeward, Windiward and other islands have not only complained but have objected to paying their share of the cost. The minister's department has had protest after protest from the governments of the West Indies in connection with this matter, and the West Indies are defaulting now where the Canadian government defaulted in the past. How can the minister urge that it was to maintain the treaty that this thing had to be gone on with? A year or two ago he would have found the West Indies tickled to death to scrap the whole thing until they could get better boats on the route.
That is one of the reasons we have called the conference-in order to reach some decision.

I would
urge on the minister that at the conference, in the interests of Canada, in the interests of the merchant marine under his own department, he fights awfully shy of subsidies to private concerns. Let the minister use the boats of the Canadian Government merchant marine; let him improve those boats or even, as the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) has said, let him build boats.
-Mr. IRVINE:	Would it aid the government in coming to a decision on this matter if the committee merely voted as much as is required to meet the contracts now in force, and no more?

I was about to
move, along that line, that item 159 be reduced by the sum of $255,000. It seems to me that in view of the fact that this matter has been discussed for the last three years at least; that we have endeavoured again and again to have the policy of the government changed; that we believe it is utterly vicious in principle to subsidize a line to operate in competition with our own merchant marine; and in view of the fact also that the minister has informed us to-night that a conference has been called to discuss the whole matter, there is no better opportunity for us to call a halt and to register our protest against the continuance of the subsidy and to ask that the policy be completely changed.

I would ask the committee to be fully seized of the attitude they are taking on this question. The difficulty is not at all in striking out a subsidy. As a matter of fact, we have certain treaty obligations with the West Indies, just as the British government has. These steamers are not competing with our marine so far as passenger traffic is concerned because the Canadian merchant marine has only a limited passenger capacity. We are now on the eve of an arrangement with the West Indies which we trust will be beneficial to both countries. Would it not then be unwise, by striking out the estimate, to abandon the method by which we are approximating this agreement with the West Indies? I do not say that we are fully living up to those treaty obligations, because we have had such an upheaval in the world that this among other things has in a measure been overlooked. But in a few weeks' time representatives of the West Indies will be coming to Canada to discuss the whole situation, and it may be that out of the conference there will evolve something in the direction of better steamship facilities with the West Indies which will not carry a

Supply-Trade and Commerce
subsidy with it. But it would hardly have any beneficial effect, while we are negotiating with them, to cripple further the facilities which at present obtain in the service between Canada and the West Indies. With me, it is not a question of striking out a subsidy; I have no interest in the Pickford & Black steamships. But these steamers are assisting in carrying out our obligations, and until we arrive at some satisfactory agreement I do not think it would be wise to adopt such a course as is now suggested.

I would
suggest to the minister that probably he would be able to enter that conference in June with much freer hands and a clearer brain, and under much less influence-although I have no idea that he would be influenced-if he cut himself adrift from this subsidy before the conference takes place. It would be the best thing for the country if this were done. The minister raises the issue of treaty obligations; but as I pointed out, the treaty obligations have been broken on both sides, and the present state of affairs is a source of irritation between the West Indies and Canada. As regards passenger accommodation, no man who wants to make a business trip to the West Indies is going to waste his time on a Pickford & Black eleven-knot old wreck of a schooner; he will go to New York or Montreal and take a fast boat. Business men have no time to waste in winter tours. As a matter of fact, the whole idea in the subsidy is to provide some nice well-off gentleman with a pleasing manner of spending a winter holiday. It is a nice long tour. As the member for Cumberland indicated, it certainly takes a longer time than any member in this House could spare for business purposes.

Mr. Chairman,
I have been out for some time and do not know exactly what has happened in my absence, but we have been discussing this matter at considerable length in the committee on Railways and Shipping, and the view has been pretty generally held that we ought to strengthen the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Unfortunately we have no boats at the present time which are fitted for this work.
Refrigerator space might be supplied.

It would take
some time.

What in the estimation of
the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry 226
Drayton) would it cost to fix one of these boats for passenger traffic?

We have already fixed two of them and they are able to carry thirty-five passengers. They have two good cabins, the rest are very poor and very small. These boats are each about thirty-five hundred tons. None of the boats in the West Indian trade are properly fixed for cold storage. We happen to have on hand in connection with the Canadian Government Merchant, Marine about $1,200,000 or $1,400,000, representing insurance which was paid upon some of the boats that were lost. This fund is in the hands of trustees, and the committee thought that the best thing to do was to get authority to use the money in providing boats to look after both passenger and freight business, but this would take some tittle time. The people on the islands, rightly or wrongly, think there should be a passenger service. I do not think we stressed the tourist business, I am frank in saying that; but on the other hand a great asset of the islands lies in their tourist business, and they are inclined to insist on it. We are doing fairly well with them in trade. At one time eighty-five per cent of the flour sold in Jamaica was American; as a result of the agreement of 1919-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-seventy-five per cent of the flour now sold there is Canadian. I think we should dlo nothing to disturb the situation until we get together. We are in default now. We want to get further concessions in their markets, and I think we are perfectly willing to give them further concessions in ours, but I do not think in the meantime we should give them any added cause of grievance in connection with this service.

Could the minister give us
any reason why we should pay a subsidy for passenger service between here and the West Indies? To me it seems unreasonable.
The subsidy is to cover passenger, freight and mail services, not passenger service alone.

Is that all the reason the
minister can give us why we should pay a subsidy for passenger service?

It would be impossible to develop trade without this subsidized line. As I understand it, the agreement was entered into in 1920 because it was necessary to provide a transportation service. Otherwise the islands would not have entered into any arrangement with us.

Does the minister mean that the islands would not have entered into the agreement unless we agreed to provide a passenger service?

The passenger service is part
of the agreement.
What I am trying to get at is, why we agreed to pay a subsidy for a passenger service. I may not have made myself clear to the minister, but that is the information I wish to get from him.
The subsidy is more particularly to cover freight service.

Yes; but when we suggest
that the merchant marine might be used, the reply of the minister is that they have not any passenger accommodation. Now I ask why should we enter into an agreement to subsidize a passenger service?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman was not on the committee and did not hear Sir Henry Thornton. He was pressed why we could not do all this at once. His view was that many of our boats were not suitable for the business, and that those which were suitable were already doing useful work in the Pacific coastal trade and in trade with the Orient and Australia. He wanted to be given time to look into the matter with a view to seeing just what he could do, and he was assured of the committee's full support to go ahead, but so far we have not heard anything from him. I understand, however, that the cabinet are to take the whole matter up this summer with representatives of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and of the islands.
How much trade does the minister think we would 'have to develop in order to return a profit to the Canadian people of $340,000, the amount of the subsidy?
I am sure my hon. friend is in a position to make that estimate just as well as I am.
Have we arrived there now?

The minister (Mr. Low) has told us that this contract ends in June. Will the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) inform us in what way we are bound by treaty with the West Indies to make it imperative that we pass this full vote?

I did not say it was
imperative, for this parliament can do anything it likes; but as a matter of fact there is a treaty between the West Indies and

Canada providing for certain passenger and freight salings at regular intervals.
But that ends in June, does it not?

No, the trade agreement does not end in June; but, as pointed out by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) the carrying out of this treaty obligation has become unsatisfactory to both parties. We believe that we can develop a much greater trade with the West Indies by sitting down around a table and talking over frankly with their representatives the whole situation. As the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) pointed out, it would not be wise-and that is my opinion-at the present time to do something else that would, to put it mildly, irritate the West Indian people when we are on the very eve of having a conference with them with the object of making a new arrangement that will be advantageous to us both. There is no question in the world that one of the first things to come up at that conference will be better steamship connection between the West Indies and Canada. While we are at the present time, and have been for years, carrying on this subsidized service, I think, even though we perhaps do not approve of this subsidy -and I agree largely with the statement that the ships in their present condition are not worthy of a very great subsidy-yet we have had this service running for some years, and right within a few weeks of the time of our meeting the West Indian representatives to discuss this whole situation, my humble opinion is that it would be unwise to do anything that would stir up any difficulty on this question of transportation, Which to my mind, will be even paramount in our discussion to the question of tariff or anything of that kind.

While I agree with the
principle of getting away from subsidies, I am afraid I cannot vote for the amendment. I know that a number of people are coming here from all parts of Canada to the conference on the 19th, people who are well posted, who know what they want, and who will ask for a better class of boats than we have today. The present boats are not equipped with refrigeration or any kind of cooling process and they are entirely inadequate to build up the trade in print between Canada and these countries. I think we had better wait until this conference takes place.

I think both the hon. member for Parkdale and the Min-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ister of Railways have not understood the amendment. The amendment does not affect the contract; it does not cut out the treaty; all it does is to make things safe for the government when tire conference is called so that the government can go into the conference without its hands tied by any contract. We are allowing enough in the vote, according to the minister's own statement, to provide for the fulfilling of the contract to the end of June. What more can we want?
Sir HENRY DR..YTON:	I am against
these votes as a rule, but I am interested in this West Indian business. Here is the trouble we are in: Suppose we had what the committee on National Railways and Shipping wanted-all this business with the Canadian National; Sir Henry Thornton would say that the Canadian National should have exactly that subsidy, or more; that it is unfair to ask a publicly operated service to carry on where a private service cannot make a profit. I know what a good market it is for us down there if we can really get hold of it, and what a splendid thing it would be if we could get a direct service between Canada and these countries and from the United Fruit; Company of the United States. It would be a splendid thing for us if we could get those fruits without that restriction. These people are willing to do all their business with us but they cannot do it so long as the great white fleet gives them a service which is far ahead of anything we are giving them. And Sir Henry Thornton, if he is going to give them anything like an adequate service, will want this subsidy.

I would point out to the
hon. member for West York that we are all interested in this contract. We are interested now to the extent of $5,000,000. The minister admits that the boats now in the service, which are receiving the subsidy, are obsolete. It is right that we should be interested in it, and if we do not take some steps to get the cabinet interested in it I suppose they will go on paying this subsidy forever and the people of Canada will go on licking stamps to put on their notes. We are preaching economy to the people; let us not set them a bad example by failing to practise it ourselves. I wish to ask the minister with whom this contract is made and to whom this money is being paid at present.

The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company.
Amendment (Mr. Woodsworth) negatived; Yeas, 13; Nays, 56.

Canada and South Africa, steam service between,
How many ships are in this service?	*

The subsidy is $25,000 less than last year. The contract is with the Elder Dempster Company. It is for a monthly service during the first fifteen days of each month, sailing from Montreal and calling at Quebec. During the months of September, October and November, the calls are at Halifax, but during the winter months the sailings are from St. John, calling at Halifax.

How many millions have
been spent on this service since it was inaugurated?

I am sorry I have not the
figures before me. I may say that as a result of this arrangement we supply about 75 per cent of the paper market of South Africa, and during the last ten years there has been little or no increase in the rates. Exports to South Africa in 1923 amounted to $5,583,390; 1924, $8,019,853; for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1925, $9,276,502. am increase of almost 100 per cent in the last two years.
Are we still paying the same subsidy?
No. The subsidy was reduced last year and again this year, and we hope gradually to wipe it out.
Are there any government merchant marine boats on this route?
No.
Are these the only boats trading between Canada and South Africa?
Yes.

It appears to me that according to this principle or lack of principle, of subsidizing, that the Canadian people are being taxed to ship goods to other countries, to the extent that they are paying more than really the whole traffic is worth in some instances, I should like to ask the minister how long he thinks Canada can be taxed to ship goods to other countries?

In selling these goods we create employment in this country, and I think the spending of $100,000 to increase our exports by 100 per cent is a good investment.

Will the minister say that the trade to South Africa has created enough extra employment in Canadla to pay for the amount of the taxes required for the subsidy?
I think so.
Are you sure of that? What are the figures?
